papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Models: Circuit-Level Analysis and Causal Validation
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models internally process and transform information during the denoising procedure, and what are the computational circuits and mechanisms underlying image generation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a quantitative circuit-level analysis framework for diffusion models, revealing systematic algorithmic differences in how they process synthetic versus naturalistic data, identifying specialized attention mechanisms, and providing causal validation through intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes the first comprehensive circuit-level analysis of diffusion models, providing quantitative foundations for mechanistic interpretability and revealing systematic algorithmic differences between synthetic and naturalistic data processing with implications for model control and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Real-world face processing requires circuits with measurably higher computational complexity than synthetic data processing, though with variability across model initializations.
Eight functionally distinct attention mechanisms with specialized computational roles (e.g., edge detection, texture analysis, semantic understanding) were identified and quantified.
Temporal activation analysis reveals distinct processing phases across the denoising process, with some attention heads specializing in early structure formation and others in detail refinement.
Intervention analysis identifies critical computational bottlenecks, with targeted ablations producing performance degradation from 25.6% to 153.8%.
Circuit transferability varies with abstraction level and temporal phase, suggesting a hierarchical organization of fundamental and domain-specific computations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on facial image generation using synthetic and CelebA datasets, which may limit generalizability to other image domains.
The model used is a 262M parameter architecture, substantially smaller than state-of-the-art diffusion models, which may limit the discovery of emergent capabilities and circuit complexity present in larger models.
While intervention analysis provides evidence for circuit functionality, more sophisticated causal analysis methods could strengthen mechanistic claims.
The correlation between attention head entropy and peak activation timing did not reach statistical significance, suggesting head specialization is multidimensional.
future_direction: Extending the circuit analysis methodologies to larger-scale diffusion models and diverse generation tasks.
Developing more sophisticated causal analysis techniques for understanding generative model computation.
Extending the methodologies to text-to-image generation and other cross-modal tasks.
papers.abstract: We present a quantitative circuit-level analysis of diffusion models, establishing computational pathways and mechanistic principles underlying image generation processes. Through systematic intervention experiments across 2,000 synthetic and 2,000 CelebA facial images, we discover fundamental algorithmic differences in how diffusion architectures process synthetic versus naturalistic data distributions. Our investigation reveals that real-world face processing requires circuits with measurably higher computational complexity (complexity ratio = 1.084 plus/minus 0.008, p < 0.001), exhibiting distinct attention specialization patterns with entropy divergence ranging from 0.015 to 0.166 across denoising timesteps. We identify eight functionally distinct attention mechanisms showing specialized computational roles: edge detection (entropy = 3.18 plus/minus 0.12), texture analysis (entropy = 4.16 plus/minus 0.08), and semantic understanding (entropy = 2.67 plus/minus 0.15). Intervention analysis demonstrates critical computational bottlenecks where targeted ablations produce 25.6% to 128.3% performance degradation, providing causal evidence for identified circuit functions. These findings establish quantitative foundations for algorithmic understanding and control of generative model behavior through mechanistic intervention strategies.

papers.title: Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing the Training Origins of Interpretable LLM Units
papers.research_question: How can we trace the training data origins of interpretable circuits in LLMs, and what causal role do specific training samples play in the formation of these circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Mechanistic Data Attribution (MDA) framework to trace training data origins of interpretable units in LLMs, and provides causal evidence linking induction heads to in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The MDA framework enables tracing training data origins of interpretable units and provides causal insights into circuit formation, with practical applications for data augmentation and model steering.
papers.key_findings:
Targeted intervention (removing or augmenting high-influence samples) significantly modulates the emergence of interpretable heads, while random interventions show no effect.
Repetitive structural data (e.g., LaTeX, XML) acts as a mechanistic catalyst for induction head formation.
High-influence samples are transferable across different induction heads, indicating mechanism-specific drivers.
Induction head formation follows a steady accumulation model, with high-influence samples primarily modulating the rate of emergence.
Interventions targeting induction head formation induce concurrent changes in the model's in-context learning capability, providing causal evidence for their functional link.
papers.limitation: The computational cost of the MDA framework is prohibitive for dense influence analysis over the entire training lifecycle.
future_direction: Investigating the complex multi-head dynamics and circuit reconfiguration in larger models.
papers.abstract: While Mechanistic Interpretability has identified interpretable circuits in LLMs, their causal origins in training data remain elusive. We introduce Mechanistic Data Attribution (MDA), a scalable framework that employs Influence Functions to trace interpretable units back to specific training samples. Through extensive experiments on the Pythia family, we causally validate that targeted intervention--removing or augmenting a small fraction of high-influence samples--significantly modulates the emergence of interpretable heads, whereas random interventions show no effect. Our analysis reveals that repetitive structural data (e.g., LaTeX, XML) acts as a mechanistic catalyst. Furthermore, we observe that interventions targeting induction head formation induce a concurrent change in the model's in-context learning (ICL) capability. This provides direct causal evidence for the long-standing hypothesis regarding the functional link between induction heads and ICL. Finally, we propose a mechanistic data augmentation pipeline that consistently accelerates circuit convergence across model scales, providing a principled methodology for steering the developmental trajectories of LLMs.

papers.title: Can Subnetwork Structure be the Key to Out-of-Distribution Generalization?
papers.research_question: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? The paper investigates whether subnetworks within biased models can achieve better OOD performance.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that biased models contain unbiased functional subnetworks, proposes the functional lottery ticket hypothesis, and introduces Modular Risk Minimization (MRM) to improve OOD generalization by learning subnetwork structures.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork structure is a key factor for out-of-distribution generalization, and the proposed Modular Risk Minimization method effectively learns such structures to improve OOD performance.
papers.key_findings:
Even biased models that exploit spurious correlations contain subnetworks that are less susceptible to these shortcuts.
The functional lottery ticket hypothesis: a full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance when trained in isolation.
Modular Risk Minimization (MRM) effectively learns subnetworks that improve OOD generalization and can be combined with other OOD methods.
Sparsity constraints alone are insufficient for OOD generalization; the structure of the subnetwork is key.
MRM and its variants consistently improve OOD performance across multiple biased datasets.
papers.limitation:
The work has not considered data settings where group attribution information is available (e.g., as in Sagawa et al., 2019).
The experiments use a label noise-free setting, which may not reflect scenarios where spurious features have higher correlation than invariant features.
future_direction: Explore combinations of MRM with different loss designs for subnetwork and model learning.
Extend the approach to data settings with group attribution available.
Investigate the relationship between the structure of digit modules and subsets found by methods like 'and mask' under more domains.
papers.abstract: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? Peters et al. (2016) provides a positive answer for linear cases. In this paper, we use a functional modular probing method to analyze deep model structures under OOD setting. We demonstrate that even in biased models (which focus on spurious correlation) there still exist unbiased functional subnetworks. Furthermore, we articulate and demonstrate the functional lottery ticket hypothesis: full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance. We then propose Modular Risk Minimization to solve the subnetwork selection problem. Our algorithm learns the subnetwork structure from a given dataset, and can be combined with any other OOD regularization methods. Experiments on various OOD generalization tasks corroborate the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: Explainable AI in drug discovery: self-interpretable graph neural network for molecular property prediction using concept whitening
papers.research_question: How can concept whitening be adapted to graph neural networks to create self-interpretable models for molecular property prediction in drug discovery, and does this improve both performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts the concept whitening (CW) interpretability method to graph neural networks, enabling self-interpretable QSAR models that align latent space axes with known molecular properties (concepts) and identify relevant structural parts of molecules for predictions.
papers.conclusion: The adaptation of concept whitening to graph neural networks provides an effective framework for building self-interpretable models in drug discovery, offering improved performance and clear insights into the molecular properties driving predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Adding concept whitening layers to GNNs improves classification performance (ROC-AUC) and interpretability on molecular property prediction tasks.
The method successfully identifies which predefined molecular properties (concepts) are most relevant for predictions at different network depths.
Two novel activation modes for CW in GNNs (weighted_topk_pool and topk_pool) are introduced and evaluated.
The choice of normalization layer (BatchNorm, InstanceNorm, LayerNorm, GraphNorm) in the base model affects the performance after adding CW layers.
The method provides both structural (via GNNExplainer) and conceptual explanations for model predictions in drug discovery.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: Analysis of Atomistic Representations Using Weighted Skip-Connections
papers.research_question: How do weighted skip-connections help in understanding the relative importance of interaction blocks in SchNet for property prediction, and how does this depend on chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sc-SchNet, a modified SchNet architecture with weighted skip-connections, enabling analysis of the relative importance of interaction blocks for property prediction, revealing dependencies on molecular structure and dataset.
papers.conclusion: sc-SchNet enables interpretable analysis of atomistic representations, showing that contribution weights vary with dataset and molecular structure, providing insights into model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
sc-SchNet performs similarly to SchNet on energy and force prediction tasks.
During training on QM9, contribution weights shift from early layers to later layers as the model learns.
For MD17 trajectories, atom type embeddings have constant contribution due to fixed chemical composition.
Higher interaction blocks are more important for larger and more flexible molecules like salicylic acid and aspirin.
The relative weighting of interaction blocks depends on the chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom of the molecules.
future_direction: Investigate if interaction coefficients encode information on locality of different molecular properties.
Explore relation to fundamental modes of molecular motion in the context of the MD17 molecules.
papers.abstract: In this work, we extend the SchNet architecture by using weighted skip connections to assemble the final representation. This enables us to study the relative importance of each interaction block for property prediction. We demonstrate on both the QM9 and MD17 dataset that their relative weighting depends strongly on the chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom of the molecules which opens the path towards a more detailed understanding of machine learning models for molecules.

papers.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts
papers.research_question: How can we explain why a language model produces a particular output for a specific input query by tracing the information flow inside the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the stability of mechanistic interpretability methods, specifically circuit discovery, and how does variance in causal mediation analysis and its approximations affect the reliability of discovered circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that circuit discovery methods are highly unstable due to intrinsic variance in causal mediation analysis scores and amplification by approximation methods, advocating for more rigorous statistical practices in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Circuit discovery is not a stable process and requires statistical rigor, including reporting stability metrics and sensitivity analyses, to become a reliable scientific tool.
papers.key_findings:
Exact causal mediation analysis (CMA) scores exhibit high intrinsic variance across inputs, meaning the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable.
Approximation methods like Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) amplify this variance, leading to low signal-to-noise ratios.
Circuit discovery pipelines are sensitive to data resampling, hyperparameters, and counterfactual definitions, resulting in structurally inconsistent circuits.
Larger models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B) show higher variability in circuit discovery compared to smaller models (e.g., gpt2-small).
The instability of circuits is not mitigated by instruction tuning (comparing Llama-3.2-1B and its instruct variant).
papers.limitation:
Focus on the EAP family of methods, leaving out newer methods that may have different properties.
Exact CMA analysis was only done on gpt2-small for the IOI task due to computational constraints.
Limited to three classic MI tasks, which may not generalize to fuzzier reasoning tasks.
Stability metrics treat all edges equally, whereas weighted metrics might reveal a stable functional core.
future_direction: Probabilistic circuit discovery: characterizing a distribution over possible circuits.
Decomposing variance into estimator variance and intrinsic variance.
Stability-aware optimization: developing objectives that explicitly optimize for stability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.

papers.title: ACES-GNN: can graph neural network learn to explain activity cliffs?
papers.research_question: Can Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) be trained to provide better explanations for activity cliffs (structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences) while also improving prediction accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ACES-GNN framework, which integrates explanation supervision for activity cliffs into GNN training, improving both predictive accuracy and the interpretability of molecular structure-property relationships.
papers.conclusion: ACES-GNN represents a promising direction for improving both the predictivity and interpretability of GNN models in QSAR applications, with the potential to accelerate lead optimization in drug discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ACES-GNN improves explainability (global direction) on 28 out of 30 datasets compared to unsupervised GNNs.
ACES-GNN improves prediction accuracy for activity cliff molecules, reducing RMSE_cliff.
A positive correlation exists between the improvement in prediction accuracy and the improvement in explanation quality.
The ACES framework is effective across different GNN backbones (MPNN, GIN, GAT).
Explanation supervision helps the model focus on uncommon substructures critical for activity cliffs, aligning attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations.
papers.limitation:
The ground-truth coloring relies on a fixed definition for activity cliff molecules, and some uncommon substructures between pairs may not be causative for potency changes.
The current GNN backbone does not outperform the Random Forest + ECFP combination in predictive accuracy or attribution quality across all datasets.
The validation process prioritizes minimizing RMSE during training rather than optimizing the explainability metric, so not all attributions after supervision achieve higher global direction accuracy.
future_direction: Incorporate geometric information into GNNs for further improvement.
Explore alternative gradient-based explanation techniques, such as expected gradients, to reduce potential biases.
Develop methods to identify true causal substructures in activity cliffs, enhancing explanation evaluation and guidance.
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have revolutionized molecular property prediction by leveraging graph-based representations, yet their opaque decision-making processes hinder broader adoption in drug discovery. This study introduces the Activity-Cliff-Explanation-Supervised GNN (ACES-GNN) framework, designed to simultaneously improve predictive accuracy and interpretability by integrating explanation supervision for activity cliffs (ACs) into GNN training. ACs, defined by structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences, pose challenges for traditional models due to their reliance on shared structural features. By aligning model attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations, the ACES-GNN framework bridges the gap between prediction and explanation. Validated across 30 pharmacological targets, ACES-GNN consistently enhances both predictive accuracy and attribution quality for ACs compared to unsupervised GNNs. Our results demonstrate a positive correlation between improved predictions and accurate explanations, offering a robust and adaptable framework to better understand and interpret ACs. This work underscores the potential of explanation-guided learning to advance interpretable artificial intelligence in molecular modeling and drug discovery.

papers.title: Desiderata for Representation Learning: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How can representation learning desiderata (non-spuriousness, efficiency, disentanglement) be formalized using causal notions, and how can metrics and algorithms be developed to learn such representations from single observational datasets?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a causal framework for representation learning that formalizes desiderata like non-spuriousness, efficiency, and disentanglement using counterfactual notions (probabilities of causation) and provides metrics and algorithms (CAUSAL-REP and IOSS) to learn such representations from single observational datasets.
papers.conclusion: Causality provides a fruitful perspective for representation learning, allowing intuitive desiderata to be formalized and leading to metrics and algorithms that can learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Non-spuriousness and efficiency in supervised representation learning can be formalized using probabilities of sufficiency (PS) and necessity (PN), leading to the CAUSAL-REP algorithm.
Disentanglement in unsupervised representation learning can be formalized via causal disentanglement, leading to the Independence-of-Support Score (IOSS) metric.
CAUSAL-REP learns non-spurious representations that improve out-of-distribution prediction on image and text datasets compared to baseline methods.
IOSS can distinguish disentangled from entangled representations better than existing unsupervised metrics on synthetic and real datasets.
The causal perspective enables the development of calculable metrics and algorithms for representation learning desiderata without requiring multiple environments or labeled features.
papers.limitation:
CAUSAL-REP requires the pinpointability condition (i.e., the unobserved common cause C can be pinpointed from X) for identification.
IOSS assumes compact support of the representation and may not apply to representations with unbounded support.
papers.abstract: Representation learning constructs low-dimensional representations to summarize essential features of high-dimensional data. This learning problem is often approached by describing various desiderata associated with learned representations; e.g., that they be non-spurious, efficient, or disentangled. It can be challenging, however, to turn these intuitive desiderata into formal criteria that can be measured and enhanced based on observed data. In this paper, we take a causal perspective on representation learning, formalizing non-spuriousness and efficiency (in supervised representation learning) and disentanglement (in unsupervised representation learning) using counterfactual quantities and observable consequences of causal assertions. This yields computable metrics that can be used to assess the degree to which representations satisfy the desiderata of interest and learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.

papers.title: Do learned representations respect causal relationships?
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether learned attribute-specific representations respect the same causal relations as the underlying attributes, and to what extent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces NCINet, a learning-based method for observational causal discovery from high-dimensional representations, and shows that learned representations can respect the causal relations between attributes, with consistency correlated to predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that learned representations can respect causal relationships under controlled scenarios, and introduces NCINet, which outperforms existing methods for causal discovery from high-dimensional representations.
papers.key_findings:
NCINet significantly outperforms existing observational causal discovery approaches on synthetic and real data.
Under controlled scenarios, learned representations can satisfy the same causal relations as the underlying attribute labels.
The causal consistency between representations and labels is positively correlated with the predictive capability of the representations.
Causal consistency degrades with overfitting of the attribute predictors.
The adversarial loss component in NCINet improves its generalization ability.
papers.abstract: Data often has many semantic attributes that are causally associated with each other. But do attribute-specific learned representations of data also respect the same causal relations? We answer this question in three steps. First, we introduce NCINet, an approach for observational causal discovery from high-dimensional data. It is trained purely on synthetically generated representations and can be applied to real representations, and is specifically designed to mitigate the domain gap between the two. Second, we apply NCINet to identify the causal relations between image representations of different pairs of attributes with known and unknown causal relations between the labels. For this purpose, we consider image representations learned for predicting attributes on the 3D Shapes, CelebA, and the CASIA-WebFace datasets, which we annotate with multiple multi-class attributes. Third, we analyze the effect on the underlying causal relation between learned representations induced by various design choices in representation learning. Our experiments indicate that (1) NCINet significantly outperforms existing observational causal discovery approaches for estimating the causal relation between pairs of random samples, both in the presence and absence of an unobserved confounder, (2) under controlled scenarios, learned representations can indeed satisfy the underlying causal relations between their respective labels, and (3) the causal relations are positively correlated with the predictive capability of the representations.

papers.title: Global Geometry Is Not Enough for Vision Representations
papers.research_question: Does global embedding geometry, commonly used to evaluate representation quality, predict compositional binding capability in vision encoders?
papers.core_contribution: Global embedding geometry does not predict compositional binding capability in vision encoders; functional sensitivity, measured by the Jacobian effective rank, is a strong predictor and reveals a gap arising from objective design.
papers.conclusion: Global embedding geometry captures only a partial view of representational competence; functional sensitivity is a critical complementary axis for modeling composite structure.
papers.key_findings:
Standard geometric metrics (e.g., isotropy, participation ratio) show near-zero correlation with compositional binding accuracy across 21 vision encoders.
Jacobian Effective Rank (JER), a measure of local input-output sensitivity, strongly correlates with binding performance.
The disparity between geometry and function arises because existing training objectives explicitly constrain global embedding geometry but leave the local input-output mapping largely unconstrained.
Variance-decorrelation objectives (e.g., Barlow Twins, VICReg) preserve high functional rank and achieve better binding, while other objectives (e.g., CLIP, MAE) exhibit functional rank collapse.
Alternative geometric readouts (kNN, local PCA) cannot recover binding information from frozen embeddings; linear accessibility is intrinsic to the pretraining objective.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted in a controlled synthetic setting to isolate compositional binding, and is not intended to exhaustively characterize all forms of structure in large-scale or naturalistic representations.
future_direction: Developing training objectives and evaluation benchmarks that target functional structure more directly than geometry-based criteria or linear probing.
papers.abstract: A common assumption in representation learning is that globally well-distributed embeddings support robust and generalizable representations. This focus has shaped both training objectives and evaluation protocols, implicitly treating global geometry as a proxy for representational competence. While global geometry effectively encodes which elements are present, it is often insensitive to how they are composed. We investigate this limitation by testing the ability of geometric metrics to predict compositional binding across 21 vision encoders. We find that standard geometry-based statistics exhibit near-zero correlation with compositional binding. In contrast, functional sensitivity, as measured by the input-output Jacobian, reliably tracks this capability. We further provide an analytic account showing that this disparity arises from objective design, as existing losses explicitly constrain embedding geometry but leave the local input-output mapping unconstrained. These results suggest that global embedding geometry captures only a partial view of representational competence and establish functional sensitivity as a critical complementary axis for modeling composite structure.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Geometric Scaling of Bayesian Inference in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do the geometric structures that enable exact Bayesian inference in wind tunnels persist in production-scale language models?
papers.core_contribution: The geometric structures (value manifolds, key orthogonality, attention focusing) that enable exact Bayesian inference in controlled settings persist in production-scale language models and are used during inference for Bayesian updating.
papers.conclusion: The geometric substrate for the inference primitives persists at scale, and content-based value routing is a stable representational bias in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Domain restriction collapses value manifolds to one-dimensional geometry, matching wind-tunnel tasks.
Production models use the geometric substrate during inference, as shown by movement along the entropy-ordered manifold in the SULA task.
Static geometric signatures (value manifolds and key orthogonality) are preserved across architectures, while dynamic attention focusing is modulated by architectural constraints.
Interventions on the entropy-aligned axis disrupt local geometry but do not proportionally degrade Bayesian-like behavior, indicating the geometry is a readout of distributed uncertainty.
papers.limitation:
Architectural coverage limited to dense MHA, GQA, and sliding-window attention; SSMs and hybrid architectures are not covered.
Scale: largest model is 12B dense and 8x7B MoE; frontier-scale models (70B-400B) are not evaluated.
Task specificity: models are general-purpose; domain-specialized models may have different geometric patterns.
Causal probes: single-layer interventions do not yield a clean causal separation; uncertainty may be distributed.
future_direction: Validate geometric signatures in frontier-scale checkpoints and alternative architectures (including SSMs).
Develop interventional methods for manipulating keys, values, or attention to test causal roles.
Track geometric evolution during training.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that small transformers trained in controlled "wind-tunnel'' settings can implement exact Bayesian inference, and that their training dynamics produce a geometric substrate -- low-dimensional value manifolds and progressively orthogonal keys -- that encodes posterior structure. We investigate whether this geometric signature persists in production-grade language models. Across Pythia, Phi-2, Llama-3, and Mistral families, we find that last-layer value representations organize along a single dominant axis whose position strongly correlates with predictive entropy, and that domain-restricted prompts collapse this structure into the same low-dimensional manifolds observed in synthetic settings. To probe the role of this geometry, we perform targeted interventions on the entropy-aligned axis of Pythia-410M during in-context learning. Removing or perturbing this axis selectively disrupts the local uncertainty geometry, whereas matched random-axis interventions leave it intact. However, these single-layer manipulations do not produce proportionally specific degradation in Bayesian-like behavior, indicating that the geometry is a privileged readout of uncertainty rather than a singular computational bottleneck. Taken together, our results show that modern language models preserve the geometric substrate that enables Bayesian inference in wind tunnels, and organize their approximate Bayesian updates along this substrate.

papers.title: When Models Manipulate Manifolds: The Geometry of a Counting Task
papers.research_question: How does Claude 3.5 Haiku perform linebreaking in fixed-width text, specifically how it represents character counts and detects line boundaries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that character counts in linebreaking are represented on low-dimensional curved manifolds, and the model performs geometric transformations (twisting, orthogonal arrangement) to detect boundaries and make linebreak decisions.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the rich sensory processing of early layers, the intricacy of attention algorithms, and the importance of combining feature-based and geometric views of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Character counts are represented on 1-dimensional feature manifolds with curvature, discretized by sparse feature families.
Attention heads 'twist' these manifolds to estimate distance to the line boundary by aligning character count and line width representations.
The decision to break the line is enabled by arranging estimates orthogonally to create a linear decision boundary.
The curvature in the character count manifold is produced by many attention heads working together in a distributed algorithm.
The model is susceptible to 'visual illusions' where certain character sequences hijack the counting mechanism.
papers.limitation:
The geometric description is expensive in researcher time and potentially limited in scope to known continuous variables.
The paper does not address how the line width is actually aggregated (e.g., max or moving average).
There are edge cases in handling tokenization and punctuation that are not fully explored.
future_direction: Extend dictionary learning to unsupervised discovery of other geometric structures.
Study other natural tasks for pretrained language models.
papers.abstract: Language models can perceive visual properties of text despite receiving only sequences of tokens-we mechanistically investigate how Claude 3.5 Haiku accomplishes one such task: linebreaking in fixed-width text. We find that character counts are represented on low-dimensional curved manifolds discretized by sparse feature families, analogous to biological place cells. Accurate predictions emerge from a sequence of geometric transformations: token lengths are accumulated into character count manifolds, attention heads twist these manifolds to estimate distance to the line boundary, and the decision to break the line is enabled by arranging estimates orthogonally to create a linear decision boundary. We validate our findings through causal interventions and discover visual illusions--character sequences that hijack the counting mechanism. Our work demonstrates the rich sensory processing of early layers, the intricacy of attention algorithms, and the importance of combining feature-based and geometric views of interpretability.

papers.title: Evaluating Brain-Inspired Modular Training in Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does modular training (BIMT) affect the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery? How does modularity impact computational efficiency (training memory, time, inference)?
papers.core_contribution: Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT) significantly improves the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery, producing sparser circuits with lower logit differences and faster discovery times, though with increased training memory and time.
papers.conclusion: BIMT is an innovative and practical approach to neural network interpretability, enabling more efficient and effective circuit discovery, which is critical for analyzing large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
BIMT achieves lower logit difference (1.2737 for circle detection) compared to other training regimes, indicating better circuit quality.
BIMT discovers circuits faster (93.76 seconds for circle detection) than other models.
BIMT produces sparser circuits (0.9859 sparsity for circle detection) which are easier to interpret.
BIMT requires more memory during training due to the swap operation, and has longer training times.
BIMT has slightly higher inference times compared to L1-only model (65.77 vs 64.65 seconds for 500000 images).
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the MNIST dataset and MLP architecture, which may not generalize to other tasks and models.
Modular training may cause neurons to become polysemantic due to superposition, which could hinder interpretability.
future_direction: Test BIMT on transformer networks.
Investigate the effect of modularity on superposition.
Use attribution patching instead of activation patching for larger networks.
Evaluate BIMT on other tasks beyond digit classification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have experienced a rapid rise in AI, changing a wide range of applications with their advanced capabilities. As these models become increasingly integral to decision-making, the need for thorough interpretability has never been more critical. Mechanistic Interpretability offers a pathway to this understanding by identifying and analyzing specific sub-networks or 'circuits' within these complex systems. A crucial aspect of this approach is Automated Circuit Discovery, which facilitates the study of large models like GPT4 or LLAMA in a feasible manner. In this context, our research evaluates a recent method, Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT), designed to enhance the interpretability of neural networks. We demonstrate how BIMT significantly improves the efficiency and quality of Automated Circuit Discovery, overcoming the limitations of manual methods. Our comparative analysis further reveals that BIMT outperforms existing models in terms of circuit quality, discovery time, and sparsity. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive computational analysis of BIMT, including aspects such as training duration, memory allocation requirements, and inference speed. This study advances the larger objective of creating trustworthy and transparent AI systems in addition to demonstrating how well BIMT works to make neural networks easier to understand.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LoRA-Adapted Language Models for Nuclear Reactor Safety Applications
papers.research_question: How does LoRA adaptation alter neuron activation patterns in an LLM for a nuclear reactor safety domain, and what is the causal role of these altered neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a methodology for tracing domain expertise in a LoRA-adapted LLM to a sparse set of neurons and demonstrates that the model's expertise is an emergent property of a neural circuit, providing a pathway for nuclear-grade AI assurance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates a replicable methodology for moving beyond treating LLMs as opaque black boxes towards a mechanistic understanding of their function, offering a pathway to achieve nuclear-grade AI assurance by identifying, monitoring, and causally testing knowledge-bearing neural circuits.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning on a BWR dataset induced systematic changes in the activation patterns of a small set of neurons in the final MLP layer.
Silencing the entire group of six key neurons collectively caused a statistically significant degradation in BLEU score, while silencing most individual neurons did not, supporting a circuit-based view of knowledge encoding.
Qualitative analysis revealed distinct functional roles for key neurons, such as encoding core technical concepts (#1066, #1086), suppressing generalist language (#941), and representing procedural logic (#176).
The adapted model produced more concise and precise answers than the base model, as measured by a decrease in average answer length and an increase in BLEU score.
The findings suggest that verifying the integrity of distributed neural circuits, rather than individual components, is crucial for safety assurance in nuclear applications.
papers.limitation: The reliance on the BLEU score, while justified for measuring output precision, does not verify factual accuracy.
future_direction: Development of domain-specific evaluation metrics that can automatically verify technical correctness against a trusted knowledge base.
Extending the methodology to other critical nuclear systems, including Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) and advanced reactor designs.
Validating the approach across different model architectures, model scales, and technical documentation corpora.
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into safety-critical domains, such as nuclear engineering, necessitates a deep understanding of their internal reasoning processes. This paper presents a novel methodology for interpreting how an LLM encodes and utilizes domain-specific knowledge, using a Boiling Water Reactor system as a case study. We adapted a general-purpose LLM (Gemma-3-1b-it) to the nuclear domain using a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique known as Low-Rank Adaptation. By comparing the neuron activation patterns of the base model to those of the fine-tuned model, we identified a sparse set of neurons whose behavior was significantly altered during the adaptation process. To probe the causal role of these specialized neurons, we employed a neuron silencing technique. Our results demonstrate that while silencing most of these specialized neurons individually did not produce a statistically significant effect, deactivating the entire group collectively led to a statistically significant degradation in task performance. Qualitative analysis further revealed that silencing these neurons impaired the model's ability to generate detailed, contextually accurate technical information. This paper provides a concrete methodology for enhancing the transparency of an opaque black-box model, allowing domain expertise to be traced to verifiable neural circuits. This offers a pathway towards achieving nuclear-grade artificial intelligence (AI) assurance, addressing the verification and validation challenges mandated by nuclear regulatory frameworks (e.g., 10 CFR 50 Appendix B), which have limited AI deployment in safety-critical nuclear operations.

papers.title: Unraveling the geometry of visual relational reasoning
papers.research_question: What mechanisms enable or constrain the generalization of abstract relations? Specifically, how are relational rules represented in neural networks, and what geometric principles govern whether they can be flexibly applied to new contexts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a geometric foundation for relational reasoning by showing that generalization is governed by the geometry of rule manifolds, and proposes SNRloss, a novel loss function that shapes representations to improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of relational reasoning in neural networks and provide testable hypotheses for how geometric principles may underlie abstract reasoning in the brain, paving the way for extending geometric analysis to broader cognitive tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SCL generalizes best among the tested models and most closely aligns with human behavior in terms of error patterns and response times.
Generalization performance is accurately predicted by geometric properties of rule manifolds: signal, dimensionality, and signal-noise overlap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals distinct strategies across models: SCL amplifies signal sharply in MLP layers, ResNet and ViT progressively refine representations, and WReN plateaus early.
A trade-off between signal and dimensionality emerges due to structured compression, where both seen and unseen rule manifolds align with a low-dimensional subspace defined by training rules.
SNRloss, a novel loss function designed to balance representation geometry, improves generalization performance compared to cross-entropy and prototypical losses.
papers.limitation: Humans have prior experience with similar rules from life, while models are trained from scratch on controlled rule splits, making direct comparison difficult.
future_direction: Develop a new benchmark for human reasoning with abstract relations unlikely to have been encountered.
Extend geometric analysis to real-world visual reasoning benchmarks and cross-modal linguistic challenges.
papers.abstract: Humans readily generalize abstract relations, such as recognizing "constant" in shape or color, whereas neural networks struggle, limiting their flexible reasoning. To investigate mechanisms underlying such generalization, we introduce SimplifiedRPM, a novel benchmark for systematically evaluating abstract relational reasoning, addressing limitations in prior datasets. In parallel, we conduct human experiments to quantify relational difficulty, enabling direct model-human comparisons. Testing four models, ResNet-50, Vision Transformer, Wild Relation Network, and Scattering Compositional Learner (SCL), we find that SCL generalizes best and most closely aligns with human behavior. Using a geometric approach, we identify key representation properties that accurately predict generalization and uncover a fundamental trade-off between signal and dimensionality: novel relations compress into training-induced subspaces. Layer-wise analysis reveals where relational structure emerges, highlights bottlenecks, and generates concrete hypotheses about abstract reasoning in the brain. Motivated by these insights, we propose SNRloss, a novel objective explicitly balancing representation geometry. Our results establish a geometric foundation for relational reasoning, paving the way for more human-like visual reasoning in AI and opening promising avenues for extending geometric analysis to broader cognitive tasks.

papers.title: Visual interpretability of image-based classification models by generative latent space disentanglement applied to in vitro fertilization
papers.research_question: How to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models in a human-interpretable way?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCOVER, a generative model that learns disentangled latent representations to discover and visualize the image properties driving classification decisions, enabling human-interpretable counterfactual explanations.
papers.conclusion: DISCOVER enables human-interpretable visual explanations for image classification models, discovers new image properties, and provides transparency for individual predictions, with potential for biological discovery.
papers.key_findings:
DISCOVER successfully identifies known blastocyst quality properties (size and trophectoderm) as classification-driving features.
DISCOVER discovers new properties (blastocoel density) that were not explicitly annotated.
DISCOVER provides instance-specific interpretation, ranking the importance of each property for individual predictions.
DISCOVER generalizes to other domains (natural images and Alzheimer's disease MRI).
DISCOVER outperforms existing interpretability methods (GradCAM, SHAP, LIME) in providing disentangled visual explanations.
papers.limitation:
One latent feature may encode multiple independent semantic image properties (entanglement).
DISCOVER may miss semantic image properties that are associated with the classification task (e.g., inner cell mass was not identified).
The method requires training a generative model, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The success of deep learning in identifying complex patterns exceeding human intuition comes at the cost of interpretability. Non-linear entanglement of image features makes deep learning a "black box" lacking human meaningful explanations for the models' decision. We present DISCOVER, a generative model designed to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models. DISCOVER learns disentangled latent representations, where each latent feature encodes a unique classification-driving visual property. This design enables "human-in-the-loop" interpretation by generating disentangled exaggerated counterfactual explanations. We apply DISCOVER to interpret classification of in vitro fertilization embryo morphology quality. We quantitatively and systematically confirm the interpretation of known embryo properties, discover properties without previous explicit measurements, and quantitatively determine and empirically verify the classification decision of specific embryo instances. We show that DISCOVER provides human-interpretable understanding of "black box" classification models, proposes hypotheses to decipher underlying biomedical mechanisms, and provides transparency for the classification of individual predictions.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: The Origins of Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are features represented as manifolds in large language models, and how does cosine similarity in representation space relate to the intrinsic geometry of features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical framework to explain representation manifolds in LLMs, showing that under the continuous correspondence hypothesis, cosine similarity encodes the intrinsic geometry of features through shortest paths on the manifold, and validates this on text embeddings and token activations.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a formal mathematical framework to explain and interpret representation manifolds in large language models, validating the theory on internal representations and text embeddings, and revealing unexpected encodings of distances.
papers.key_findings:
Representation manifolds in LLMs reflect the topology of features (e.g., colors and dates form loops, years form a curve) as predicted by the continuous correspondence hypothesis.
Cosine similarity between feature representations locally reflects distance in the feature metric space, implying isometry up to scaling.
Years in GPT2-small are encoded on a logarithmic scale rather than linear, with larger distances between more recent years.
For colors in text-embedding-large-3, the representations follow a hue cycle rather than other possible encodings like RGB.
The manifold geometry allows linear computation of functions of the feature value, supporting the superposition hypothesis.
papers.limitation:
The hypothesis-driven approach is manual and not scalable, relying on a reasonable starting hypothesis for the metric space.
PCA may not capture the full complexity of distances encoded by the language model, which might be more complex and not correspond to human understanding.
Estimating manifolds in the presence of noise is statistically difficult, and the K-nearest-neighbour graph approach is prone to short-circuits causing errors.
future_direction: Learning the metric automatically rather than manual hypothesis
Developing 'manifold-aware' sparse autoencoders
Using the metric space formalism in future scientific discourse
papers.abstract: There is a large ongoing scientific effort in mechanistic interpretability to map embeddings and internal representations of AI systems into human-understandable concepts. A key element of this effort is the linear representation hypothesis, which posits that neural representations are sparse linear combinations of `almost-orthogonal' direction vectors, reflecting the presence or absence of different features. This model underpins the use of sparse autoencoders to recover features from representations. Moving towards a fuller model of features, in which neural representations could encode not just the presence but also a potentially continuous and multidimensional value for a feature, has been a subject of intense recent discourse. We describe why and how a feature might be represented as a manifold, demonstrating in particular that cosine similarity in representation space may encode the intrinsic geometry of a feature through shortest, on-manifold paths, potentially answering the question of how distance in representation space and relatedness in concept space could be connected. The critical assumptions and predictions of the theory are validated on text embeddings and token activations of large language models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can disentangled representations be identified without relying on statistical assumptions, by using mechanistic independence criteria?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework for disentangled representations based on mechanistic independence, proposing several independence criteria and proving identifiability theorems for latent subspaces under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic independence provides a unifying framework that clarifies the conditions for identifiability of disentangled representations without relying on statistical assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
Local disentanglement implies global disentanglement under mild topological conditions (path-connectedness and local injectivity).
Type D independence (disjoint support) yields identifiability of latent subspaces up to block-wise invertible transforms and permutations.
Type M independence (mutual non-inclusion) yields identifiability when combined with a sparsity regularizer.
Type S independence (sparsity gap) yields identifiability even when supports overlap.
Type Hn independence (vanishing cross-derivatives) yields identifiability when the generator is separable of order n.
papers.limitation: The sparsity gap condition (Type S) is intractable to optimize in practice, and finding robust surrogate losses is an open problem.
future_direction: Identifying robust surrogate losses for the sparsity gap condition (Type S).
papers.abstract: Disentangled representations seek to recover latent factors of variation underlying observed data, yet their identifiability is still not fully understood. We introduce a unified framework in which disentanglement is achieved through mechanistic independence, which characterizes latent factors by how they act on observed variables rather than by their latent distribution. This perspective is invariant to changes of the latent density, even when such changes induce statistical dependencies among factors. Within this framework, we propose several related independence criteria -- ranging from support-based and sparsity-based to higher-order conditions -- and show that each yields identifiability of latent subspaces, even under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing. We further establish a hierarchy among these criteria and provide a graph-theoretic characterization of latent subspaces as connected components. Together, these results clarify the conditions under which disentangled representations can be identified without relying on statistical assumptions.

papers.title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the dual problem to interpretability? The paper introduces patterning as the dual: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data leads to it.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces patterning as the dual of interpretability, using susceptibilities to derive data interventions that steer internal structure formation in neural networks, demonstrated in small language models and a synthetic task.
papers.conclusion: Patterning provides a principled approach to steering generalization by inverting the susceptibility relationship, with potential applications to AI alignment and control of internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting training data along the second principal susceptibility direction can accelerate or delay the formation of the induction circuit.
In the parentheses balancing task, patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution.
Susceptibility-guided interventions produce predictable changes in internal structures.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use small models (3M parameters) and simple tasks.
Susceptibility estimation is computationally expensive.
Focus on one-off interventions made at the start of training, not online control.
