These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Geometric Scaling of Bayesian Inference in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do the geometric structures that enable exact Bayesian inference in wind tunnels persist in production-scale language models?
papers.core_contribution: The geometric structures (value manifolds, key orthogonality, attention focusing) that enable exact Bayesian inference in controlled settings persist in production-scale language models and are used during inference for Bayesian updating.
papers.conclusion: The geometric substrate for the inference primitives persists at scale, and content-based value routing is a stable representational bias in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Domain restriction collapses value manifolds to one-dimensional geometry, matching wind-tunnel tasks.
Production models use the geometric substrate during inference, as shown by movement along the entropy-ordered manifold in the SULA task.
Static geometric signatures (value manifolds and key orthogonality) are preserved across architectures, while dynamic attention focusing is modulated by architectural constraints.
Interventions on the entropy-aligned axis disrupt local geometry but do not proportionally degrade Bayesian-like behavior, indicating the geometry is a readout of distributed uncertainty.
papers.limitation:
Architectural coverage limited to dense MHA, GQA, and sliding-window attention; SSMs and hybrid architectures are not covered.
Scale: largest model is 12B dense and 8x7B MoE; frontier-scale models (70B-400B) are not evaluated.
Task specificity: models are general-purpose; domain-specialized models may have different geometric patterns.
Causal probes: single-layer interventions do not yield a clean causal separation; uncertainty may be distributed.
future_direction: Validate geometric signatures in frontier-scale checkpoints and alternative architectures (including SSMs).
Develop interventional methods for manipulating keys, values, or attention to test causal roles.
Track geometric evolution during training.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that small transformers trained in controlled "wind-tunnel'' settings can implement exact Bayesian inference, and that their training dynamics produce a geometric substrate -- low-dimensional value manifolds and progressively orthogonal keys -- that encodes posterior structure. We investigate whether this geometric signature persists in production-grade language models. Across Pythia, Phi-2, Llama-3, and Mistral families, we find that last-layer value representations organize along a single dominant axis whose position strongly correlates with predictive entropy, and that domain-restricted prompts collapse this structure into the same low-dimensional manifolds observed in synthetic settings. To probe the role of this geometry, we perform targeted interventions on the entropy-aligned axis of Pythia-410M during in-context learning. Removing or perturbing this axis selectively disrupts the local uncertainty geometry, whereas matched random-axis interventions leave it intact. However, these single-layer manipulations do not produce proportionally specific degradation in Bayesian-like behavior, indicating that the geometry is a privileged readout of uncertainty rather than a singular computational bottleneck. Taken together, our results show that modern language models preserve the geometric substrate that enables Bayesian inference in wind tunnels, and organize their approximate Bayesian updates along this substrate.

papers.title: When Models Manipulate Manifolds: The Geometry of a Counting Task
papers.research_question: How does Claude 3.5 Haiku perform linebreaking in fixed-width text, specifically how it represents character counts and detects line boundaries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that character counts in linebreaking are represented on low-dimensional curved manifolds, and the model performs geometric transformations (twisting, orthogonal arrangement) to detect boundaries and make linebreak decisions.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the rich sensory processing of early layers, the intricacy of attention algorithms, and the importance of combining feature-based and geometric views of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Character counts are represented on 1-dimensional feature manifolds with curvature, discretized by sparse feature families.
Attention heads 'twist' these manifolds to estimate distance to the line boundary by aligning character count and line width representations.
The decision to break the line is enabled by arranging estimates orthogonally to create a linear decision boundary.
The curvature in the character count manifold is produced by many attention heads working together in a distributed algorithm.
The model is susceptible to 'visual illusions' where certain character sequences hijack the counting mechanism.
papers.limitation:
The geometric description is expensive in researcher time and potentially limited in scope to known continuous variables.
The paper does not address how the line width is actually aggregated (e.g., max or moving average).
There are edge cases in handling tokenization and punctuation that are not fully explored.
future_direction: Extend dictionary learning to unsupervised discovery of other geometric structures.
Study other natural tasks for pretrained language models.
papers.abstract: Language models can perceive visual properties of text despite receiving only sequences of tokens-we mechanistically investigate how Claude 3.5 Haiku accomplishes one such task: linebreaking in fixed-width text. We find that character counts are represented on low-dimensional curved manifolds discretized by sparse feature families, analogous to biological place cells. Accurate predictions emerge from a sequence of geometric transformations: token lengths are accumulated into character count manifolds, attention heads twist these manifolds to estimate distance to the line boundary, and the decision to break the line is enabled by arranging estimates orthogonally to create a linear decision boundary. We validate our findings through causal interventions and discover visual illusions--character sequences that hijack the counting mechanism. Our work demonstrates the rich sensory processing of early layers, the intricacy of attention algorithms, and the importance of combining feature-based and geometric views of interpretability.

papers.title: Evaluating Brain-Inspired Modular Training in Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does modular training (BIMT) affect the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery? How does modularity impact computational efficiency (training memory, time, inference)?
papers.core_contribution: Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT) significantly improves the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery, producing sparser circuits with lower logit differences and faster discovery times, though with increased training memory and time.
papers.conclusion: BIMT is an innovative and practical approach to neural network interpretability, enabling more efficient and effective circuit discovery, which is critical for analyzing large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
BIMT achieves lower logit difference (1.2737 for circle detection) compared to other training regimes, indicating better circuit quality.
BIMT discovers circuits faster (93.76 seconds for circle detection) than other models.
BIMT produces sparser circuits (0.9859 sparsity for circle detection) which are easier to interpret.
BIMT requires more memory during training due to the swap operation, and has longer training times.
BIMT has slightly higher inference times compared to L1-only model (65.77 vs 64.65 seconds for 500000 images).
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the MNIST dataset and MLP architecture, which may not generalize to other tasks and models.
Modular training may cause neurons to become polysemantic due to superposition, which could hinder interpretability.
future_direction: Test BIMT on transformer networks.
Investigate the effect of modularity on superposition.
Use attribution patching instead of activation patching for larger networks.
Evaluate BIMT on other tasks beyond digit classification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have experienced a rapid rise in AI, changing a wide range of applications with their advanced capabilities. As these models become increasingly integral to decision-making, the need for thorough interpretability has never been more critical. Mechanistic Interpretability offers a pathway to this understanding by identifying and analyzing specific sub-networks or 'circuits' within these complex systems. A crucial aspect of this approach is Automated Circuit Discovery, which facilitates the study of large models like GPT4 or LLAMA in a feasible manner. In this context, our research evaluates a recent method, Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT), designed to enhance the interpretability of neural networks. We demonstrate how BIMT significantly improves the efficiency and quality of Automated Circuit Discovery, overcoming the limitations of manual methods. Our comparative analysis further reveals that BIMT outperforms existing models in terms of circuit quality, discovery time, and sparsity. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive computational analysis of BIMT, including aspects such as training duration, memory allocation requirements, and inference speed. This study advances the larger objective of creating trustworthy and transparent AI systems in addition to demonstrating how well BIMT works to make neural networks easier to understand.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LoRA-Adapted Language Models for Nuclear Reactor Safety Applications
papers.research_question: How does LoRA adaptation alter neuron activation patterns in an LLM for a nuclear reactor safety domain, and what is the causal role of these altered neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a methodology for tracing domain expertise in a LoRA-adapted LLM to a sparse set of neurons and demonstrates that the model's expertise is an emergent property of a neural circuit, providing a pathway for nuclear-grade AI assurance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates a replicable methodology for moving beyond treating LLMs as opaque black boxes towards a mechanistic understanding of their function, offering a pathway to achieve nuclear-grade AI assurance by identifying, monitoring, and causally testing knowledge-bearing neural circuits.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning on a BWR dataset induced systematic changes in the activation patterns of a small set of neurons in the final MLP layer.
Silencing the entire group of six key neurons collectively caused a statistically significant degradation in BLEU score, while silencing most individual neurons did not, supporting a circuit-based view of knowledge encoding.
Qualitative analysis revealed distinct functional roles for key neurons, such as encoding core technical concepts (#1066, #1086), suppressing generalist language (#941), and representing procedural logic (#176).
The adapted model produced more concise and precise answers than the base model, as measured by a decrease in average answer length and an increase in BLEU score.
The findings suggest that verifying the integrity of distributed neural circuits, rather than individual components, is crucial for safety assurance in nuclear applications.
papers.limitation: The reliance on the BLEU score, while justified for measuring output precision, does not verify factual accuracy.
future_direction: Development of domain-specific evaluation metrics that can automatically verify technical correctness against a trusted knowledge base.
Extending the methodology to other critical nuclear systems, including Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) and advanced reactor designs.
Validating the approach across different model architectures, model scales, and technical documentation corpora.
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into safety-critical domains, such as nuclear engineering, necessitates a deep understanding of their internal reasoning processes. This paper presents a novel methodology for interpreting how an LLM encodes and utilizes domain-specific knowledge, using a Boiling Water Reactor system as a case study. We adapted a general-purpose LLM (Gemma-3-1b-it) to the nuclear domain using a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique known as Low-Rank Adaptation. By comparing the neuron activation patterns of the base model to those of the fine-tuned model, we identified a sparse set of neurons whose behavior was significantly altered during the adaptation process. To probe the causal role of these specialized neurons, we employed a neuron silencing technique. Our results demonstrate that while silencing most of these specialized neurons individually did not produce a statistically significant effect, deactivating the entire group collectively led to a statistically significant degradation in task performance. Qualitative analysis further revealed that silencing these neurons impaired the model's ability to generate detailed, contextually accurate technical information. This paper provides a concrete methodology for enhancing the transparency of an opaque black-box model, allowing domain expertise to be traced to verifiable neural circuits. This offers a pathway towards achieving nuclear-grade artificial intelligence (AI) assurance, addressing the verification and validation challenges mandated by nuclear regulatory frameworks (e.g., 10 CFR 50 Appendix B), which have limited AI deployment in safety-critical nuclear operations.

papers.title: Unraveling the geometry of visual relational reasoning
papers.research_question: What mechanisms enable or constrain the generalization of abstract relations? Specifically, how are relational rules represented in neural networks, and what geometric principles govern whether they can be flexibly applied to new contexts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a geometric foundation for relational reasoning by showing that generalization is governed by the geometry of rule manifolds, and proposes SNRloss, a novel loss function that shapes representations to improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of relational reasoning in neural networks and provide testable hypotheses for how geometric principles may underlie abstract reasoning in the brain, paving the way for extending geometric analysis to broader cognitive tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SCL generalizes best among the tested models and most closely aligns with human behavior in terms of error patterns and response times.
Generalization performance is accurately predicted by geometric properties of rule manifolds: signal, dimensionality, and signal-noise overlap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals distinct strategies across models: SCL amplifies signal sharply in MLP layers, ResNet and ViT progressively refine representations, and WReN plateaus early.
A trade-off between signal and dimensionality emerges due to structured compression, where both seen and unseen rule manifolds align with a low-dimensional subspace defined by training rules.
SNRloss, a novel loss function designed to balance representation geometry, improves generalization performance compared to cross-entropy and prototypical losses.
papers.limitation: Humans have prior experience with similar rules from life, while models are trained from scratch on controlled rule splits, making direct comparison difficult.
future_direction: Develop a new benchmark for human reasoning with abstract relations unlikely to have been encountered.
Extend geometric analysis to real-world visual reasoning benchmarks and cross-modal linguistic challenges.
papers.abstract: Humans readily generalize abstract relations, such as recognizing "constant" in shape or color, whereas neural networks struggle, limiting their flexible reasoning. To investigate mechanisms underlying such generalization, we introduce SimplifiedRPM, a novel benchmark for systematically evaluating abstract relational reasoning, addressing limitations in prior datasets. In parallel, we conduct human experiments to quantify relational difficulty, enabling direct model-human comparisons. Testing four models, ResNet-50, Vision Transformer, Wild Relation Network, and Scattering Compositional Learner (SCL), we find that SCL generalizes best and most closely aligns with human behavior. Using a geometric approach, we identify key representation properties that accurately predict generalization and uncover a fundamental trade-off between signal and dimensionality: novel relations compress into training-induced subspaces. Layer-wise analysis reveals where relational structure emerges, highlights bottlenecks, and generates concrete hypotheses about abstract reasoning in the brain. Motivated by these insights, we propose SNRloss, a novel objective explicitly balancing representation geometry. Our results establish a geometric foundation for relational reasoning, paving the way for more human-like visual reasoning in AI and opening promising avenues for extending geometric analysis to broader cognitive tasks.

papers.title: Visual interpretability of image-based classification models by generative latent space disentanglement applied to in vitro fertilization
papers.research_question: How to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models in a human-interpretable way?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCOVER, a generative model that learns disentangled latent representations to discover and visualize the image properties driving classification decisions, enabling human-interpretable counterfactual explanations.
papers.conclusion: DISCOVER enables human-interpretable visual explanations for image classification models, discovers new image properties, and provides transparency for individual predictions, with potential for biological discovery.
papers.key_findings:
DISCOVER successfully identifies known blastocyst quality properties (size and trophectoderm) as classification-driving features.
DISCOVER discovers new properties (blastocoel density) that were not explicitly annotated.
DISCOVER provides instance-specific interpretation, ranking the importance of each property for individual predictions.
DISCOVER generalizes to other domains (natural images and Alzheimer's disease MRI).
DISCOVER outperforms existing interpretability methods (GradCAM, SHAP, LIME) in providing disentangled visual explanations.
papers.limitation:
One latent feature may encode multiple independent semantic image properties (entanglement).
DISCOVER may miss semantic image properties that are associated with the classification task (e.g., inner cell mass was not identified).
The method requires training a generative model, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The success of deep learning in identifying complex patterns exceeding human intuition comes at the cost of interpretability. Non-linear entanglement of image features makes deep learning a "black box" lacking human meaningful explanations for the models' decision. We present DISCOVER, a generative model designed to discover the underlying visual properties driving image-based classification models. DISCOVER learns disentangled latent representations, where each latent feature encodes a unique classification-driving visual property. This design enables "human-in-the-loop" interpretation by generating disentangled exaggerated counterfactual explanations. We apply DISCOVER to interpret classification of in vitro fertilization embryo morphology quality. We quantitatively and systematically confirm the interpretation of known embryo properties, discover properties without previous explicit measurements, and quantitatively determine and empirically verify the classification decision of specific embryo instances. We show that DISCOVER provides human-interpretable understanding of "black box" classification models, proposes hypotheses to decipher underlying biomedical mechanisms, and provides transparency for the classification of individual predictions.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: The Origins of Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are features represented as manifolds in large language models, and how does cosine similarity in representation space relate to the intrinsic geometry of features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical framework to explain representation manifolds in LLMs, showing that under the continuous correspondence hypothesis, cosine similarity encodes the intrinsic geometry of features through shortest paths on the manifold, and validates this on text embeddings and token activations.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a formal mathematical framework to explain and interpret representation manifolds in large language models, validating the theory on internal representations and text embeddings, and revealing unexpected encodings of distances.
papers.key_findings:
Representation manifolds in LLMs reflect the topology of features (e.g., colors and dates form loops, years form a curve) as predicted by the continuous correspondence hypothesis.
Cosine similarity between feature representations locally reflects distance in the feature metric space, implying isometry up to scaling.
Years in GPT2-small are encoded on a logarithmic scale rather than linear, with larger distances between more recent years.
For colors in text-embedding-large-3, the representations follow a hue cycle rather than other possible encodings like RGB.
The manifold geometry allows linear computation of functions of the feature value, supporting the superposition hypothesis.
papers.limitation:
The hypothesis-driven approach is manual and not scalable, relying on a reasonable starting hypothesis for the metric space.
PCA may not capture the full complexity of distances encoded by the language model, which might be more complex and not correspond to human understanding.
Estimating manifolds in the presence of noise is statistically difficult, and the K-nearest-neighbour graph approach is prone to short-circuits causing errors.
future_direction: Learning the metric automatically rather than manual hypothesis
Developing 'manifold-aware' sparse autoencoders
Using the metric space formalism in future scientific discourse
papers.abstract: There is a large ongoing scientific effort in mechanistic interpretability to map embeddings and internal representations of AI systems into human-understandable concepts. A key element of this effort is the linear representation hypothesis, which posits that neural representations are sparse linear combinations of `almost-orthogonal' direction vectors, reflecting the presence or absence of different features. This model underpins the use of sparse autoencoders to recover features from representations. Moving towards a fuller model of features, in which neural representations could encode not just the presence but also a potentially continuous and multidimensional value for a feature, has been a subject of intense recent discourse. We describe why and how a feature might be represented as a manifold, demonstrating in particular that cosine similarity in representation space may encode the intrinsic geometry of a feature through shortest, on-manifold paths, potentially answering the question of how distance in representation space and relatedness in concept space could be connected. The critical assumptions and predictions of the theory are validated on text embeddings and token activations of large language models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can disentangled representations be identified without relying on statistical assumptions, by using mechanistic independence criteria?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework for disentangled representations based on mechanistic independence, proposing several independence criteria and proving identifiability theorems for latent subspaces under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic independence provides a unifying framework that clarifies the conditions for identifiability of disentangled representations without relying on statistical assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
Local disentanglement implies global disentanglement under mild topological conditions (path-connectedness and local injectivity).
Type D independence (disjoint support) yields identifiability of latent subspaces up to block-wise invertible transforms and permutations.
Type M independence (mutual non-inclusion) yields identifiability when combined with a sparsity regularizer.
Type S independence (sparsity gap) yields identifiability even when supports overlap.
Type Hn independence (vanishing cross-derivatives) yields identifiability when the generator is separable of order n.
papers.limitation: The sparsity gap condition (Type S) is intractable to optimize in practice, and finding robust surrogate losses is an open problem.
future_direction: Identifying robust surrogate losses for the sparsity gap condition (Type S).
papers.abstract: Disentangled representations seek to recover latent factors of variation underlying observed data, yet their identifiability is still not fully understood. We introduce a unified framework in which disentanglement is achieved through mechanistic independence, which characterizes latent factors by how they act on observed variables rather than by their latent distribution. This perspective is invariant to changes of the latent density, even when such changes induce statistical dependencies among factors. Within this framework, we propose several related independence criteria -- ranging from support-based and sparsity-based to higher-order conditions -- and show that each yields identifiability of latent subspaces, even under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing. We further establish a hierarchy among these criteria and provide a graph-theoretic characterization of latent subspaces as connected components. Together, these results clarify the conditions under which disentangled representations can be identified without relying on statistical assumptions.

papers.title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the dual problem to interpretability? The paper introduces patterning as the dual: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data leads to it.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces patterning as the dual of interpretability, using susceptibilities to derive data interventions that steer internal structure formation in neural networks, demonstrated in small language models and a synthetic task.
papers.conclusion: Patterning provides a principled approach to steering generalization by inverting the susceptibility relationship, with potential applications to AI alignment and control of internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting training data along the second principal susceptibility direction can accelerate or delay the formation of the induction circuit.
In the parentheses balancing task, patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution.
Susceptibility-guided interventions produce predictable changes in internal structures.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use small models (3M parameters) and simple tasks.
Susceptibility estimation is computationally expensive.
Focus on one-off interventions made at the start of training, not online control.
Theoretical framework assumes infinitesimal perturbations, while practical interventions are finite; understanding when the linear approximation breaks down is important.
Connection between observables and downstream behavior (e.g., safety properties) requires further study.
future_direction: Develop online control (adjusting data distribution dynamically during training).
Scale to larger models and more efficient methods.
Study the connection to safety properties and AI alignment applications.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how neural networks generalize beyond their training data by reverse-engineering their internal structures. We introduce patterning as the dual problem: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data produces it. Our approach is based on susceptibilities, which measure how posterior expectation values of observables respond to infinitesimal shifts in the data distribution. Inverting this linear response relationship yields the data intervention that steers the model toward a target internal configuration. We demonstrate patterning in a small language model, showing that re-weighting training data along principal susceptibility directions can accelerate or delay the formation of structure, such as the induction circuit. In a synthetic parentheses balancing task where multiple algorithms achieve perfect training accuracy, we show that patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution. These results establish that the same mathematical framework used to read internal structure can be inverted to write it.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Low-Complexity Probing via Finding Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Can we develop a probing method that is more faithful to a pre-trained model's internal representations (i.e., better at finding encoded properties and less able to learn tasks on its own) and offers a better accuracy-complexity tradeoff than standard MLP probes?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces subnetwork probing, a subtractive pruning-based probing method that finds an existing subnetwork within a frozen pre-trained model to perform a linguistic task. It is shown to be more faithful (higher accuracy on pre-trained models, lower on random models) and Pareto-dominant in accuracy-complexity tradeoff compared to standard MLP probes.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork probing is a more faithful and informative probing method than existing approaches, offering a better accuracy-complexity tradeoff and enabling additional analysis of where tasks are encoded within a model.
papers.key_findings:
Subnetwork probing achieves higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models than MLP probes, indicating it is better at finding encoded properties and less able to learn tasks independently.
Subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing, achieving higher accuracy for any given probe complexity budget.
Analysis of the extracted subnetworks shows that lower-level linguistic tasks (e.g., part-of-speech tagging) are captured in lower layers of the model, reproducing findings from prior work.
future_direction: Applying neuron explainability techniques to the subnetworks found by the method.
papers.abstract: The dominant approach in probing neural networks for linguistic properties is to train a new shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on top of the model's internal representations. This approach can detect properties encoded in the model, but at the cost of adding new parameters that may learn the task directly. We instead propose a subtractive pruning-based probe, where we find an existing subnetwork that performs the linguistic task of interest. Compared to an MLP, the subnetwork probe achieves both higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models, so it is both better at finding properties of interest and worse at learning on its own. Next, by varying the complexity of each probe, we show that subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing in that it achieves higher accuracy given any budget of probe complexity. Finally, we analyze the resulting subnetworks across various tasks to locate where each task is encoded, and we find that lower-level tasks are captured in lower layers, reproducing similar findings in past work.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unveiling of Transformer Circuits: Self-Influence as a Key to Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: What multi-step reasoning mechanisms are used by language models to solve tasks?
papers.core_contribution: We propose the Self-Influence Circuit Analysis Framework (SICAF) to trace and analyze the thought processes of language models during complex reasoning tasks by combining circuit analysis and self-influence functions.
papers.conclusion: The SICAF framework successfully maps hierarchical reasoning pathways in GPT-2 for the IOI task, revealing a human-like reasoning structure and enhancing model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SICAF framework can trace and analyze the thought processes of LMs in complex reasoning tasks.
Circuits identified for the IOI task are small (1-2% of edges) and faithful (recover ≥85% of model performance).
EAP-IG and EAP-IG-KL outperform EAP in normalized faithfulness and converge with fewer parameters.
The model's key parameters for the IOI task are concentrated in the first and last few layers.
The model follows a hierarchical reasoning path: identifying entities in early layers, interpreting actions in middle layers, and synthesizing information in final layers.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was conducted primarily on the GPT-2 model and may not generalize to larger or different architectures without adaptation.
Calculating self-influence requires computationally intensive methods, which may pose scalability challenges for more complex models.
The work focused on a single task (Indirect Object Identification, or IOI), and the applicability of these findings to other natural language processing tasks remains an open question.
future_direction: Explore the adaptability of the approach across varied tasks and model architectures.
Investigate methods to optimize computational efficiency of self-influence calculation.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Analyzing Atomic Interactions in Molecules as Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: To what extent do machine learning force fields (MLFFs) such as SchNet and PaiNN learn underlying physicochemical concepts from data, and how well do their predictions align with known chemical principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops an explainable AI (XAI) framework based on GNN-LRP to analyze atomic interactions in machine learning force fields, and finds that models deviating from fundamental chemical principles produce unstable molecular dynamics trajectories despite high prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed XAI framework provides a way to understand and improve machine learning force fields by assessing their adherence to chemical principles, which is crucial for generating stable and physically meaningful simulations.
papers.key_findings:
Interaction strength is atom-type and property dependent.
Intensive properties (e.g., HOMO energy) have a larger interaction range than extensive properties (e.g., atomization energy).
The decay of interaction strength with distance does not follow a polynomial power law as expected from physical principles.
Models exhibit many-body interactions, meaning interaction strength between two atoms depends on the chemical neighborhood.
Models that deviate too far from chemical principles, even with low test errors, produce unstable molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.limitation: The analysis is specific to graph neural networks with a cutoff distance, and the framework's computational complexity is high for large numbers of layers, though approximations mitigate this.
future_direction: Improving ML architectures to better account for the polynomial decay of atomic interactions.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures and a wider range of molecular properties.
papers.abstract: While machine learning (ML) models have been able to achieve unprecedented accuracies across various prediction tasks in quantum chemistry, it is now apparent that accuracy on a test set alone is not a guarantee for robust chemical modeling such as stable molecular dynamics (MD). To go beyond accuracy, we use explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques to develop a general analysis framework for atomic interactions and apply it to the SchNet and PaiNN neural network models. We compare these interactions with a set of fundamental chemical principles to understand how well the models have learned the underlying physicochemical concepts from the data. We focus on the strength of the interactions for different atomic species, how predictions for intensive and extensive quantum molecular properties are made, and analyze the decay and many-body nature of the interactions with interatomic distance. Models that deviate too far from known physical principles produce unstable MD trajectories, even when they have very high energy and force prediction accuracy. We also suggest further improvements to the ML architectures to better account for the polynomial decay of atomic interactions.

papers.title: Interpretable and Explainable Machine Learning for Materials Science and Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability and explainability techniques be applied to machine learning models in materials science and chemistry to improve scientific discovery, build trust, and unveil correlations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper summarizes applications of interpretability and explainability techniques for materials science and chemistry, discussing how these techniques can improve scientific studies by providing insights beyond predictive power, building trust, and revealing unexpected correlations.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning is crucial for realizing the true potential of ML in materials science, and human experts who embrace interpretable ML will replace those who do not.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability in scientific machine learning involves trade-offs between explainability, completeness, and scientific validity (correctness).
Intrinsically interpretable models (e.g., linear models, decision trees) offer direct interpretations but may lack correctness for complex phenomena.
Extrinsic interpretation methods (e.g., SHAP, salience maps, attention mechanisms) can provide insights for complex models like deep neural networks.
Interpretability techniques can generate scientific hypotheses and guide experiments, but they require careful validation to avoid over-interpretation and confusion with causation.
Future directions include integrating uncertainty estimates into explanations and combining machine learning with causal inference for more robust insights.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability methods may lead to over-interpretation, especially when searching for physical explanations, and can be misled by shortcut learning or unrealistic feature combinations.
Explanations from machine learning models do not have strong causal guarantees and are susceptible to confounding effects, requiring secondary confirmation by experiments or simulation.
There is a trade-off between interpretability, completeness, and correctness in model explanations, meaning no single explanation may fully capture the model's operation and physical reality.
future_direction: Integrating uncertainty estimates into model explanations to improve confidence in insights.
Combining machine learning with causal inference to uncover cause-and-effect relationships from materials data.
Using advanced methods like autoencoders and sparse regression to directly extract physical knowledge from noisy experimental data.
papers.abstract:
While the uptake of data-driven approaches for materials science and
chemistry is at an exciting, early stage, to realise the true potential of
machine learning models for successful scientific discovery, they must have
qualities beyond purely predictive power. The predictions and inner workings of
models should provide a certain degree of explainability by human experts,
permitting the identification of potential model issues or limitations,
building trust on model predictions and unveiling unexpected correlations that
may lead to scientific insights. In this work, we summarize applications of
interpretability and explainability techniques for materials science and
chemistry and discuss how these techniques can improve the outcome of
scientific studies. We discuss various challenges for interpretable machine
learning in materials science and, more broadly, in scientific settings. In
particular, we emphasize the risks of inferring causation or reaching
generalization by purely interpreting machine learning models and the need of
uncertainty estimates for model explanations. Finally, we showcase a number of
exciting developments in other fields that could benefit interpretability in
material science and chemistry problems.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Improving Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks in Medical Diagnosis by Investigating the Individual Units
papers.research_question: How can attribution techniques like LRP and RAP improve the interpretability of DNNs in medical diagnosis by visualizing significant factors and revealing inconsistencies between human and DNN intentions?
papers.core_contribution: Attribution methods like LRP and RAP can effectively localize lesions in chest X-rays without bounding box supervision and reveal that DNNs may learn based on normal lung features rather than disease lesions, highlighting the need for interpretability in medical diagnosis.
papers.conclusion: Attribution techniques such as LRP and RAP offer efficient ways to interpret DNN decisions in medical diagnosis by localizing lesions and uncovering potential inconsistencies, underscoring the necessity of explainability for reliable adoption.
papers.key_findings:
LRP and RAP achieve higher IOU scores than CAM for localizing lesions in chest X-ray images, indicating better visualization accuracy.
Attribution methods provide detailed pixel-wise explanations compared to CAM's broad visualizations from resized feature maps.
DNNs trained for pneumonia classification may focus on normal lung features rather than pneumonia lesions, showing inconsistency with human intentions.
CheXNet, pretrained for multiple diseases, provides clear visual explanations aligned with lesion areas, unlike models trained only on pneumonia data.
The study emphasizes the importance of explainability to ensure DNNs' decision criteria align with clinical expectations.
papers.abstract: As interpretability has been pointed out as the obstacle to the adoption of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), there is an increasing interest in solving a transparency issue to guarantee the impressive performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficiency of recent attribution techniques to explain the diagnostic decision by visualizing the significant factors in the input image. By utilizing the characteristics of objectness that DNNs have learned, fully decomposing the network prediction visualizes clear localization of target lesion. To verify our work, we conduct our experiments on Chest X-ray diagnosis with publicly accessible datasets. As an intuitive assessment metric for explanations, we report the performance of intersection of Union between visual explanation and bounding box of lesions. Experiment results show that recently proposed attribution methods visualize the more accurate localization for the diagnostic decision compared to the traditionally used CAM. Furthermore, we analyze the inconsistency of intentions between humans and DNNs, which is easily obscured by high performance. By visualizing the relevant factors, it is possible to confirm that the criterion for decision is in line with the learning strategy. Our analysis of unmasking machine intelligence represents the necessity of explainability in the medical diagnostic decision.

papers.title: Structural Causality-based Generalizable Concept Discovery Models
papers.research_question: How can task-specific concepts be learned from disentangled generative factors using a structural causal model?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a variational autoencoder-based disentanglement method combined with a structural causal model to learn task-specific concepts from generative factors.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully identifies causal relationships between generative factors and task-specific concepts, opening doors for future research unifying disentanglement and causal discovery of concepts.
papers.key_findings:
The method learns disentangled latent representations with competitive MIC scores compared to supervised and unsupervised VAE baselines.
The learned causal matrix successfully identifies relevant generative factors for downstream tasks, with thresholding and regularization improving accuracy.
A trade-off exists between task accuracy and disentanglement performance, controlled by the classification loss weight hyperparameter δ.
The method generalizes to tasks with different numbers of relevant generative factors (2-GF and 3-GF).
Reconstruction quality is maintained while learning task-specific concepts.
future_direction: Future research unifying disentanglement and causal discovery of concepts.
papers.abstract: The rising need for explainable deep neural network architectures has utilized semantic concepts as explainable units. Several approaches utilizing disentangled representation learning estimate the generative factors and utilize them as concepts for explaining DNNs. However, even though the generative factors for a dataset remain fixed, concepts are not fixed entities and vary based on downstream tasks. In this paper, we propose a disentanglement mechanism utilizing a variational autoencoder (VAE) for learning mutually independent generative factors for a given dataset and subsequently learning task-specific concepts using a structural causal model (SCM). Our method assumes generative factors and concepts to form a bipartite graph, with directed causal edges from generative factors to concepts. Experiments are conducted on datasets with known generative factors: D-sprites and Shapes3D. On specific downstream tasks, our proposed method successfully learns task-specific concepts which are explained well by the causal edges from the generative factors. Lastly, separate from current causal concept discovery methods, our methodology is generalizable to an arbitrary number of concepts and flexible to any downstream tasks.

papers.title: Attacks Meet Interpretability: Attribute-steered Detection of\n Adversarial Samples
papers.research_question: How can we detect adversarial samples in face recognition models by leveraging the interpretability of DNNs, specifically by examining whether model predictions are based on human-perceptible attributes?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel adversarial sample detection technique for face recognition models based on interpretability, featuring bi-directional correspondence inference between face attributes and internal neurons, and neuron strengthening/weakening.
papers.conclusion: AmI is an effective adversarial sample detection technique for face recognition models that leverages interpretability through bi-directional attribute-neuron correspondence inference and model transformation.
papers.key_findings:
AmI achieves 94% detection accuracy for 7 different adversarial attacks with 9.91% false positives on benign inputs, outperforming the state-of-the-art feature squeezing technique.
Bi-directional reasoning (attribute substitution and preservation) is critical for extracting high-quality attribute witnesses and achieving good detection performance.
The technique is robust to the exclusion of witnesses for individual attributes, with detection accuracy degrading by less than 5% in most cases.
Attribute-steered model transformation (neuron strengthening and weakening) effectively amplifies the reasoning part of the computation and suppresses the uninterpretable part for detection.
The extracted attribute witnesses are of high quality, achieving higher accuracy in attribute detection than using the face descriptor layer of VGG-Face.
papers.abstract:
Adversarial sample attacks perturb benign inputs to induce DNN misbehaviors.
Recent research has demonstrated the widespread presence and the devastating
consequences of such attacks. Existing defense techniques either assume prior
knowledge of specific attacks or may not work well on complex models due to
their underlying assumptions. We argue that adversarial sample attacks are
deeply entangled with interpretability of DNN models: while classification
results on benign inputs can be reasoned based on the human perceptible
features/attributes, results on adversarial samples can hardly be explained.
Therefore, we propose a novel adversarial sample detection technique for face
recognition models, based on interpretability. It features a novel
bi-directional correspondence inference between attributes and internal neurons
to identify neurons critical for individual attributes. The activation values
of critical neurons are enhanced to amplify the reasoning part of the
computation and the values of other neurons are weakened to suppress the
uninterpretable part. The classification results after such transformation are
compared with those of the original model to detect adversaries. Results show
that our technique can achieve 94% detection accuracy for 7 different kinds of
attacks with 9.91% false positives on benign inputs. In contrast, a
state-of-the-art feature squeezing technique can only achieve 55% accuracy with
23.3% false positives.

papers.title: Hierarchical Sparse Circuit Extraction from Billion-Parameter Language Models through Scalable Attribution Graph Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can sparse computational circuits be efficiently extracted from billion-parameter language models using hierarchical decomposition and attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD), a framework that reduces circuit discovery complexity from exponential to polynomial, enabling extraction of interpretable circuits from billion-parameter models with high behavioral preservation.
papers.conclusion: HAGD enables circuit extraction from large models with preserved behavior, but limitations include incomplete attention modeling, reconstruction residuals, and interpretability challenges for large circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HAGD reduces circuit discovery complexity to O(n^2 log n) and extracts circuits from models up to 70B parameters.
Behavioral preservation ranges from 82% to 97% on algorithmic tasks and 74% to 88% on natural language benchmarks.
Cross-architecture transfer shows 52%-82% structural similarity, indicating shared computational patterns.
Circuit size grows sublinearly with model parameters, but natural language tasks yield larger, less modular circuits.
The method outperforms baselines like ACDC in scalability while maintaining comparable circuit quality.
papers.limitation:
Attention circuits are not modeled, leaving significant computational pathways unanalyzed.
Reconstruction dark matter of 15-20% unexplained variance means extracted circuits are incomplete.
Validation circularity arises from using ablation experiments that assume circuit completeness.
GNN meta-model requires ground-truth circuit labels that are expensive to obtain.
Large circuits with hundreds of nodes may exceed human interpretability limits.
future_direction: Integrate attention and MLP circuit analysis.
Characterize reconstruction residuals (dark matter).
Develop label-efficient training methods for GNN meta-model.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations into human-understandable algorithms, yet extracting sparse computational circuits from billion-parameter language models remains challenging due to exponential search complexity and pervasive polysemanticity. The proposed Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD) framework reduces circuit discovery complexity from O(2^n) exhaustive enumeration to O(n^2 log n) through multi-resolution abstraction hierarchies and differentiable circuit search. The methodology integrates cross-layer transcoders for monosemantic feature extraction, graph neural network meta-learning for topology prediction, and causal intervention protocols for validation. Empirical evaluation spans GPT-2 variants, Llama-7B through Llama-70B, and Pythia suite models across algorithmic tasks and natural language benchmarks. On modular arithmetic tasks, the framework achieves up to 91% behavioral preservation ($\pm$2.3\% across runs) while maintaining interpretable subgraph sizes. Cross-architecture transfer experiments suggest that discovered circuits exhibit moderate structural similarity (averaging 67%) across model families, indicating potential shared computational patterns.
