These results provide preliminary foundations for interpretability at larger model scales while identifying significant limitations in current attribution methodologies that require future advances.

papers.title: Latent Functional Maps: a spectral framework for representation alignment
papers.research_question: How can we model the relation between distinct representational spaces of neural models using spectral geometry to enable comparison, correspondence finding, and transfer of representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Latent Functional Maps, a spectral framework for aligning and comparing neural network representations, enabling interpretable similarity measurement, correspondence finding, and transfer of representations across models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Latent Functional Maps provide a versatile spectral framework for comparing, aligning, and transferring neural network representations, effective even with few or no anchors.
papers.key_findings:
LFM similarity measure is robust to perturbations that preserve linear separability, unlike CKA.
LFM enables effective zero-shot stitching of neural network components with very few anchors, outperforming orthogonal transformation baselines.
LFM significantly improves retrieval performance (MRR) with as few as 5 anchors.
LFM can operate with supervised, weakly supervised, and unsupervised descriptors, including label information without anchors.
The framework is versatile, validated on image and text modalities across multiple datasets.
papers.abstract: Neural models learn data representations that lie on low-dimensional manifolds, yet modeling the relation between these representational spaces is an ongoing challenge. By integrating spectral geometry principles into neural modeling, we show that this problem can be better addressed in the functional domain, mitigating complexity, while enhancing interpretability and performances on downstream tasks. To this end, we introduce a multi-purpose framework to the representation learning community, which allows to: (i) compare different spaces in an interpretable way and measure their intrinsic similarity; (ii) find correspondences between them, both in unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, and (iii) to effectively transfer representations between distinct spaces. We validate our framework on various applications, ranging from stitching to retrieval tasks, and on multiple modalities, demonstrating that Latent Functional Maps can serve as a swiss-army knife for representation alignment.

papers.title: Depth-Wise Emergence of Prediction-Centric Geometry in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do decoder-only large language models transform context into predictions, and how does representational geometry reorganize across depth to enable selective causal control over token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Decoder-only LLMs exhibit a depth-wise transition from context-processing to prediction-forming phases, with late-layer representations implementing a structured geometric code where angular organization parametrizes prediction similarity and norms encode context-specific information, providing a mechanistic-geometric account of prediction formation.
papers.conclusion: The paper reconciles geometric and intervention-based approaches by showing that late-layer angular geometry is causally operative for prediction, while early-layer geometry is descriptive but not causally relevant, highlighting the importance of targeting causally meaningful geometric degrees of freedom for model interpretation and control.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers are sensitive to input-centric interventions, while late layers are sensitive to prediction-centric interventions, indicating a functional dissociation.
There is a sharp depth-wise transition from context-processing to prediction-forming computation, accompanied by a reorganization of representational geometry.
In late layers, angular distance between representations correlates with prediction similarity (symmetric KL divergence), while Euclidean distance does not.
Purely angular interventions are effective in late layers but not in early layers, whereas norm interventions are ineffective throughout, showing that angular geometry is causally relevant for prediction.
The geometry of late-layer representations is organized such that angular structure parametrizes prediction distributions, while representation norms encode context-specific information that does not determine prediction.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single class of tasks and model architectures; unclear how broadly the identified geometric schema generalizes across tasks, modalities, or training regimes.
The relationship between early-layer context geometry (e.g., dimensionality expansion) and the emergence of prediction-aligned angular codes is not yet understood.
Analysis emphasizes representations averaged across contexts and does not address context-dependent dynamics in multi-step or algorithmic tasks.
future_direction: Understanding architectural and optimization biases that favor angular coding in prediction-forming layers.
Exploring geometry-aware, layer-specific adapters for model control.
Generalizing the findings across tasks, modalities, and training regimes, and studying context-dependent dynamics in multi-step tasks.
papers.abstract: We show that decoder-only large language models exhibit a depth-wise transition from context-processing to prediction-forming phases of computation accompanied by a reorganization of representational geometry. Using a unified framework combining geometric analysis with mechanistic intervention, we demonstrate that late-layer representations implement a structured geometric code that enables selective causal control over token prediction. Specifically, angular organization of the representation geometry parametrizes prediction distributional similarity, while representation norms encode context-specific information that does not determine prediction. Together, these results provide a mechanistic-geometric account of the dynamics of transforming context into predictions in LLMs.

papers.title: Understanding the patterns that neural networks learn from chemical spectra
papers.research_question: How does a neural network learn to classify infrared spectra of small organic molecules by functional groups, and what specific patterns (both intuitive and non-intuitive) does it use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a simpler 1D CNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance for functional group classification in infrared spectra and introduces a two-step explainability approach, revealing the network uses both characteristic group frequencies and non-intuitive patterns like tails and overtones.
papers.conclusion: The simplified CNN model is effective for spectral classification, and the explainability approach reveals the network uses both intuitive and non-intuitive spectral patterns, which can help assess generalization and guide future model design incorporating physics-based knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The 1D CNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models while being significantly less complex.
The model consistently attends to the same spectral regions across different random initializations, indicating robust feature learning.
The network learns to use characteristic group frequencies (peaks) for classification, aligning with expert knowledge.
The network also uses non-intuitive patterns such as tails and anharmonic vibrations (overtones and combination bands) to improve classification certainty.
For some functional groups (e.g., nitriles), class imbalance and the presence of only one characteristic band lead to poor classification accuracy, highlighting dataset limitations.
papers.limitation:
Class imbalance leads to poor classification accuracy for rare functional groups like nitriles.
The network sometimes uses non-characteristic vibrations (e.g., C-H wags for halides) which may not generalize to new datasets.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based intuition into model design, e.g., using IR tables to initialize parameters or filters that optimally recognize peaks.
Transfer understanding from pretrained models to new datasets (potentially from different spectral regions).
papers.abstract: We train a convolutional neural network to classify functional groups from infrared spectra. With explainability methods, we show the model uses the presence and absence of peaks, at fundamental and anharmonic frequencies for accurate classification.

papers.title: Causality-Induced Positional Encoding for Transformer-Based Representation Learning of Non-Sequential Features
papers.research_question: How can transformer architectures be extended to data with non-sequential yet causally-related features by generating positional encodings that capture underlying causal structure without predefined feature order?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CAPE, a method to generate causality-aware positional encodings for transformers on non-sequential yet causally-related features, eliminating the need for predefined order and incorporating causal structure via hyperbolic embedding of learned causal graphs.
papers.conclusion: CAPE successfully extends transformer-based representation learning to non-sequential data by incorporating causal structure into positional encodings, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements across multiple omics domains.
papers.key_findings:
CAPE effectively identifies underlying causal structure and preserves it in hyperbolic embeddings, encoding causal strength as pairwise distance and causal specificity as distance to origin.
CAPE-generated rotary positional encodings exhibit causal distance-induced attention attenuation and causal generality-induced attention attenuation, as theoretically proven.
CAPE enhances transformer performance on real-world multi-omics tasks including gene perturbation prediction, cell type annotation, cell clustering, and age prediction.
The attention scores computed with CAPE are robust to positional disturbances caused by measurement errors, as shown theoretically and empirically.
Ablation studies show the importance of hyperparameters like DAG pruning threshold, k-hop neighborhood size, and causal generality regularization weight.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness relies on the quality of the inferred causal graph, which may be inaccurate in extremely noisy or undersampled settings.
Assumes feature-wise causal structure is static across samples, which may not capture sample-specific heterogeneity in highly dynamic systems.
future_direction: Incorporating uncertainty-aware causal discovery.
Adapting CAPE to sample-dependent causal structures.
papers.abstract: Positional encoding is essential for supplementing transformer with positional information of tokens. Existing positional encoding methods demand predefined token/feature order, rendering them unsuitable for real-world data with non-sequential yet causally-related features. To address this limitation, we propose CAPE, a novel method that identifies underlying causal structure over non-sequential features as a weighted directed acyclic graph (DAG) using generalized structural equation modeling. The DAG is then embedded in hyperbolic space where its geometric structure is well-preserved using a hyperboloid model-based approach that effectively captures two important causal graph properties (causal strength & causal specificity). This step yields causality-aware positional encodings for the features, which are converted into their rotary form for integrating with transformer's self-attention mechanism. Theoretical analysis reveals that CAPE-generated rotary positional encodings possess three valuable properties for enhanced self-attention, including causal distance-induced attenuation, causal generality-induced attenuation, and robustness to positional disturbances. We evaluate CAPE over both synthetic and real-word datasets, empirically demonstrating its theoretical properties and effectiveness in enhancing transformer for data with non-sequential features. Our code is available at https://github.com/Catchxu/CAPE.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Task structure and nonlinearity jointly determine learned representational geometry
papers.research_question: How do activation function, input structure, and output structure jointly determine the learned representational geometry in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The activation function (Tanh vs ReLU) has a strong impact on learned representational geometry: Tanh networks align representations with target output geometry, while ReLU networks retain more input geometry, due to differences in symmetry and asymptotic behavior.
papers.conclusion: The activation function plays a crucial role in determining whether learned representations align more with target output geometry or input geometry, shedding light on the interplay between input-output geometry, nonlinearity, and learned representations.
papers.key_findings:
Tanh networks learn representations that reflect the structure of target outputs, while ReLU networks retain more information about input structure.
This difference is consistent across a broad class of parameterized tasks with varying input-output alignment.
The difference arises from asymmetric asymptotic behavior of ReLU leading to feature neuron specialization, while Tanh's symmetry causes neurons to inherit task label structure.
When target outputs are low-dimensional, Tanh networks produce more disentangled representations than ReLU networks.
The findings generalize to multi-layer networks and convolutional networks on image classification tasks.
future_direction: Investigate the progression of target/input alignment across layers in multi-layer networks for easy vs. hard tasks.
In-depth characterization of the effect of high input noise on target alignment in ReLU networks.
papers.abstract: The utility of a learned neural representation depends on how well its geometry supports performance in downstream tasks. This geometry depends on the structure of the inputs, the structure of the target outputs, and the architecture of the network. By studying the learning dynamics of networks with one hidden layer, we discovered that the network's activation function has an unexpectedly strong impact on the representational geometry: Tanh networks tend to learn representations that reflect the structure of the target outputs, while ReLU networks retain more information about the structure of the raw inputs. This difference is consistently observed across a broad class of parameterized tasks in which we modulated the degree of alignment between the geometry of the task inputs and that of the task labels. We analyzed the learning dynamics in weight space and show how the differences between the networks with Tanh and ReLU nonlinearities arise from the asymmetric asymptotic behavior of ReLU, which leads feature neurons to specialize for different regions of input space. By contrast, feature neurons in Tanh networks tend to inherit the task label structure. Consequently, when the target outputs are low dimensional, Tanh networks generate neural representations that are more disentangled than those obtained with a ReLU nonlinearity. Our findings shed light on the interplay between input-output geometry, nonlinearity, and learned representations in neural networks.

papers.title: Peering inside the black box: Learning the relevance of many-body functions in Neural Network potentials
papers.research_question: How can machine learned coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks be interpreted in terms of physically meaningful many-body contributions to the total energy?
papers.core_contribution: Extends GNN-LRP to interpret coarse-grained neural network potentials, showing the learned energy can be decomposed into physically meaningful many-body contributions.
papers.conclusion: GNN-LRP provides a way to interpret machine learned coarse-grained potentials, showing the learned interactions are physically meaningful and offering insights into molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
For methane and water, 2-body relevance scores show repulsive interactions at short distances and, for water, stabilizing interactions at the first solvation shell.
3-body interactions are crucial for water to recover structural properties, with relevance scores indicating stabilizing and destabilizing contributions.
For protein NTL9, relevance scores identify stabilizing interactions in the folded state and can distinguish between two folding pathways.
The method can analyze the effect of mutations by changing bead embeddings, showing the model learns amino-acid specific interactions.
Different GNN architectures (PaiNN and SO3Net) learn similar underlying physical interactions despite different functional representations.
future_direction: Refining the concepts to provide greater insight and systematic choice of architecture and functionalization.
papers.abstract: Machine learned potentials are becoming a popular tool to define an effective energy model for complex systems, either incorporating electronic structure effects at the atomistic resolution, or effectively renormalizing part of the atomistic degrees of freedom at a coarse-grained resolution. One of the main criticisms to machine learned potentials is that the energy inferred by the network is not as interpretable as in more traditional approaches where a simpler functional form is used. Here we address this problem by extending tools recently proposed in the nascent field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks (GNN). We demonstrate the approach on three different coarse-grained systems including two fluids (methane and water) and the protein NTL9. On these examples, we show that the neural network potentials can be in practice decomposed in relevance contributions to different orders, that can be directly interpreted and provide physical insights on the systems of interest.

papers.title: The Computational Complexity of Circuit Discovery for Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the computational complexity of circuit discovery queries for inner interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a complexity analysis of circuit discovery queries, showing that many are intractable (NP-hard, Σp2-hard, etc.), but also identifies tractable relaxations such as quasi-minimal circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuit discovery for inner interpretability is computationally challenging, but identifies tractable relaxations and provides a framework for understanding the complexity of interpretability queries.
papers.key_findings:
Many circuit discovery queries (e.g., sufficient circuit, circuit ablation) are NP-hard or Σp2-hard.
Some queries remain fixed-parameter intractable (W[1]-hard) even when parameterizing by model depth or other features.
Some queries are inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes.
There is a formal separation between local and global query complexity, which helps explain interpretability illusions.
Quasi-minimal circuit queries are tractable (PTIME) and retain useful affordances for description and control.
future_direction: Empirical and formal characterization of learned weights to inform average-case analyses.
Exploring more parameters for fixed-parameter tractability in circuit discovery queries.
Designing queries that rely on mid-level abstractions to bridge circuits and human-intelligible algorithms.
papers.abstract: Many proposed applications of neural networks in machine learning, cognitive/brain science, and society hinge on the feasibility of inner interpretability via circuit discovery. This calls for empirical and theoretical explorations of viable algorithmic options. Despite advances in the design and testing of heuristics, there are concerns about their scalability and faithfulness at a time when we lack understanding of the complexity properties of the problems they are deployed to solve. To address this, we study circuit discovery with classical and parameterized computational complexity theory: (1) we describe a conceptual scaffolding to reason about circuit finding queries in terms of affordances for description, explanation, prediction and control; (2) we formalize a comprehensive set of queries for mechanistic explanation, and propose a formal framework for their analysis; (3) we use it to settle the complexity of many query variants and relaxations of practical interest on multi-layer perceptrons. Our findings reveal a challenging complexity landscape. Many queries are intractable, remain fixed-parameter intractable relative to model/circuit features, and inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes. To navigate this landscape, we prove there exist transformations to tackle some of these hard problems with better-understood heuristics, and prove the tractability or fixed-parameter tractability of more modest queries which retain useful affordances. This framework allows us to understand the scope and limits of interpretability queries, explore viable options, and compare their resource demands on existing and future architectures.

papers.title: Learning local discrete features in explainable-by-design convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design a convolutional neural network that is both high-performance and explainable by using a lateral inhibition mechanism to learn local discrete features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ExplaiNet, an explainable-by-design CNN that uses a lateral inhibition layer to learn local discrete feature vectors, enabling high accuracy and providing explanations via a probabilistic graph and motif discovery.
papers.conclusion: The ExplaiNet framework breaks the performance-explainability trade-off by introducing an explainable-by-design CNN that retains or surpasses baseline performance while providing causal explanations based on discrete feature motifs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ExplaiNet model achieves comparable or better performance than baseline ResNet and DenseNet architectures on tiny image datasets while providing explanations.
The lateral inhibition layer amplifies gradients of winner neurons, leading to ordered activations and the formation of local discrete feature vectors.
Feature motif discovery using the EXTREME algorithm reduces the vocabulary of local discrete features, providing concise explanations.
The explainer probabilistic graph can infer causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs.
Experiments show that the explainer can sometimes correctly classify samples that the neural predictor misclassifies, suggesting potential for ensemble use or adversarial sample detection.
papers.limitation:
Further research on regularization aspects of the lateral inhibition function is required to investigate the magnitude of weights and activations during training.
Experiments are limited to tiny image datasets due to computational resources; the method has not been tested on medium-resolution images or high numbers of classes.
future_direction: Investigate the proper amount of weight decay and restriction of input values for positively monotonic gradient amplification in the lateral inhibition function.
Scale up the method to train models on medium-resolution images, high number of classes, and with millions of parameters.
Adjust the EXTREME algorithm to support custom numeric system bases, making the conversion to the quaternary system optional.
papers.abstract: Our proposed framework attempts to break the trade-off between performance and explainability by introducing an explainable-by-design convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the lateral inhibition mechanism. The ExplaiNet model consists of the predictor, that is a high-accuracy CNN with residual or dense skip connections, and the explainer probabilistic graph that expresses the spatial interactions of the network neurons. The value on each graph node is a local discrete feature (LDF) vector, a patch descriptor that represents the indices of antagonistic neurons ordered by the strength of their activations, which are learned with gradient descent. Using LDFs as sequences we can increase the conciseness of explanations by repurposing EXTREME, an EM-based sequence motif discovery method that is typically used in molecular biology. Having a discrete feature motif matrix for each one of intermediate image representations, instead of a continuous activation tensor, allows us to leverage the inherent explainability of Bayesian networks. By collecting observations and directly calculating probabilities, we can explain causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs. Moreover, experiments on various tiny image benchmark datasets confirm that our predictor ensures the same level of performance as the baseline architecture for a given count of parameters and/or layers. Our novel method shows promise to exceed this performance while providing an additional stream of explanations. In the solved MNIST classification task, it reaches a comparable to the state-of-the-art performance for single models, using standard training setup and 0.75 million parameters.

papers.title: EAP-GP: Mitigating Saturation Effect in Gradient-based Automated Circuit Identification
papers.research_question: How can saturation effects in gradient-based automated circuit identification methods be mitigated to improve attribution reliability and circuit faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EAP-GP, a gradient-based circuit identification method that uses a dynamically adjusted integration path (GradPath) to mitigate saturation effects, leading to more reliable edge attributions and more faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: EAP-GP effectively mitigates saturation effects in gradient-based circuit identification by using a dynamically adjusted integration path, leading to enhanced edge attribution accuracy and circuit faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-GP outperforms previous gradient-based methods (EAP and EAP-IG) in circuit faithfulness across six tasks, achieving improvements up to 17.7%.
EAP-GP maintains excellent performance on larger models (GPT-2 Medium and GPT-2 XL).
EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than existing methods when compared to manually annotated ground-truth circuits.
The method's performance is robust with only a few steps (k=4 or 5) in the GradPath construction.
EAP-GP is approximately five times slower than EAP-IG due to the additional forward and backward passes required for path construction.
papers.limitation:
EAP-GP is approximately five times slower than EAP-IG due to the additional forward and backward passes required for constructing the integration path.
Increasing the number of steps (k) in EAP-GP beyond an optimal point (e.g., k>5) can lead to performance degradation due to noise accumulation in the integration path near the corrupted input.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of transformer-based language models remains challenging. Mechanistic interpretability based on circuit discovery aims to reverse engineer neural networks by analyzing their internal processes at the level of computational subgraphs. In this paper, we revisit existing gradient-based circuit identification methods and find that their performance is either affected by the zero-gradient problem or saturation effects, where edge attribution scores become insensitive to input changes, resulting in noisy and unreliable attribution evaluations for circuit components. To address the saturation effect, we propose Edge Attribution Patching with GradPath (EAP-GP), EAP-GP introduces an integration path, starting from the input and adaptively following the direction of the difference between the gradients of corrupted and clean inputs to avoid the saturated region. This approach enhances attribution reliability and improves the faithfulness of circuit identification. We evaluate EAP-GP on 6 datasets using GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and GPT-2 XL. Experimental results demonstrate that EAP-GP outperforms existing methods in circuit faithfulness, achieving improvements up to 17.7%. Comparisons with manually annotated ground-truth circuits demonstrate that EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than previous approaches, highlighting its effectiveness in identifying accurate circuits.

papers.title: Interpreting Equivariant Representations
papers.research_question: How can we properly interpret equivariant latent representations, and how can we obtain invariant representations from equivariant models to avoid misleading conclusions and improve downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the importance of considering the inductive bias of equivariant models when interpreting latent representations and provides principles for choosing invariant projections to obtain unambiguous and informative invariant representations, which improve downstream analysis.
papers.conclusion: Invariant projections are essential for the proper interpretation and utilization of equivariant latent representations, and the proposed tools—isometric cross sections and random invariant projections—effectively address the inherent ambiguity, leading to more reliable downstream analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Equivariant latent representations are ambiguous because each input maps to a set of latent vectors (an orbit) under the group action, leading to ill-defined distances and potentially misleading visualizations and analyses.
Invariant projections, such as sorting for permutation-equivariant representations or random invariant linear projections for rotation-equivariant representations, can extract invariant features that preserve information and improve downstream task performance.
For permutation-equivariant VAEs, an isometric invariant representation obtained by sorting the latent coordinates forms a convex cone, enabling meaningful linear interpolation between molecules.
For rotation-equivariant classifiers, random invariant projections retain a high degree of information and yield latent spaces with clear structure, improving visualization and kNN classification accuracy.
The ambiguity observed in strictly equivariant models also appears in standard deep learning models where invariance is encouraged via data augmentation, highlighting the broader relevance of the issue.
papers.limitation: Choosing a suitable invariant mapping may not always be clear and can depend greatly on the model architecture.
future_direction: Suggesting suitable high-quality invariant mappings relevant for widely applied equivariant architectures.
papers.abstract: Latent representations are used extensively for downstream tasks, such as visualization, interpolation or feature extraction of deep learning models. Invariant and equivariant neural networks are powerful and well-established models for enforcing inductive biases. In this paper, we demonstrate that the inductive bias imposed on the by an equivariant model must also be taken into account when using latent representations. We show how not accounting for the inductive biases leads to decreased performance on downstream tasks, and vice versa, how accounting for inductive biases can be done effectively by using an invariant projection of the latent representations. We propose principles for how to choose such a projection, and show the impact of using these principles in two common examples: First, we study a permutation equivariant variational auto-encoder trained for molecule graph generation; here we show that invariant projections can be designed that incur no loss of information in the resulting invariant representation. Next, we study a rotation-equivariant representation used for image classification. Here, we illustrate how random invariant projections can be used to obtain an invariant representation with a high degree of retained information. In both cases, the analysis of invariant latent representations proves superior to their equivariant counterparts. Finally, we illustrate that the phenomena documented here for equivariant neural networks have counterparts in standard neural networks where invariance is encouraged via augmentation. Thus, while these ambiguities may be known by experienced developers of equivariant models, we make both the knowledge as well as effective tools to handle the ambiguities available to the broader community.

papers.title: nDNA -- the Semantic Helix of Artificial Cognition
papers.research_question: How can we characterize and compare the latent semantic genomes of diverse LLMs? What geometric invariants define model ancestry, inheritance, and epistemic divergence?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Neural DNA (nDNA) as a semantic-genotypic representation that captures the latent identity of foundation models through the intrinsic geometry of belief, integrating spectral curvature, thermodynamic length, and belief gradients to form a diagnostic framework for neural genomics.
papers.conclusion: Proposes nDNA and Neural Genomics as a framework for understanding the evolving anatomy of artificial cognition, offering a grammar for diagnosing and governing model lineage, drift, and internal alignment.
papers.abstract: As AI foundation models grow in capability, a deeper question emerges: What shapes their internal cognitive identity -- beyond fluency and output? Benchmarks measure behavior, but the soul of a model resides in its latent geometry. In this work, we propose Neural DNA (nDNA) as a semantic-genotypic representation that captures this latent identity through the intrinsic geometry of belief. At its core, nDNA is synthesized from three principled and indispensable dimensions of latent geometry: spectral curvature, which reveals the curvature of conceptual flow across layers; thermodynamic length, which quantifies the semantic effort required to traverse representational transitions through layers; and belief vector field, which delineates the semantic torsion fields that guide a model's belief directional orientations. Like biological DNA, it encodes ancestry, mutation, and semantic inheritance, found in finetuning and alignment scars, cultural imprints, and architectural drift. In naming it, we open a new field: Neural Genomics, where models are not just tools, but digital semantic organisms with traceable inner cognition. Modeling statement. We read AI foundation models as semantic fluid dynamics: meaning is transported through layers like fluid in a shaped conduit; nDNA is the physics-grade readout of that flow -- a geometry-first measure of how meaning is bent, paid for, and pushed -- yielding a stable, coordinate-free neural DNA fingerprint tied to on-input behavior; with this fingerprint we cross into biology: tracing lineages across pretraining, fine-tuning, alignment, pruning, distillation, and merges; measuring inheritance between checkpoints; detecting drift as traits shift under new data or objectives; and, ultimately, studying the evolution of artificial cognition to compare models, diagnose risks, and govern change over time.

papers.title: Making Reasoning Matter: Measuring and Improving Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: To what degree are the final answers of large language models faithful to their stated chain-of-thought reasoning steps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FRODO, a framework to improve the faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models, and uses causal mediation analysis to measure faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The paper performs a causal mediation analysis showing variation in faithfulness across LLMs and introduces FRODO, which improves faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning in small LMs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not reliably use their intermediate reasoning steps when generating an answer.
Instruction-tuned models have a stronger causal effect of reasoning steps on the final answer than RLHF-trained models.
FRODO outperforms strong baselines on four reasoning tasks, improving accuracy by 2-3% over standard fine-tuning.
FRODO improves robustness, showing a 4.5% improvement in controlled indirect effect, and generalizes better to out-of-distribution test sets.
FRODO's rationales are more faithful to its final answer predictions than standard supervised fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The causal analysis metric does not evaluate the model's real internal reasoning process.
The method requires additional counterfactual data generated by LLMs, which can be expensive.
Training time increases as training Direct Preference Optimization is a two-step process.
Experiments were run with only 3 random seeds due to complexity.
FRODO is dependent on rationales generated by LLMs, so extra care is needed in production environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to perform better when asked to reason step-by-step before answering a question. However, it is unclear to what degree the model's final answer is faithful to the stated reasoning steps. In this paper, we perform a causal mediation analysis on twelve LLMs to examine how intermediate reasoning steps generated by the LLM influence the final outcome and find that LLMs do not reliably use their intermediate reasoning steps when generating an answer. To address this issue, we introduce FRODO, a framework to tailor small-sized LMs to generate correct reasoning steps and robustly reason over these steps. FRODO consists of an inference module that learns to generate correct reasoning steps using an implicit causal reward function and a reasoning module that learns to faithfully reason over these intermediate inferences using a counterfactual and causal preference objective. Our experiments show that FRODO significantly outperforms four competitive baselines. Furthermore, FRODO improves the robustness and generalization ability of the reasoning LM, yielding higher performance on out-of-distribution test sets. Finally, we find that FRODO's rationales are more faithful to its final answer predictions than standard supervised fine-tuning.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Finetunes Small Subnetworks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the extent and causes of parameter update sparsity induced by reinforcement learning fine-tuning in large language models, comparing it to supervised fine-tuning.
papers.core_contribution: Reinforcement learning fine-tuning in large language models updates only a small, sparse subnetwork of parameters (5%-30%) without explicit sparsity constraints, and fine-tuning this subnetwork alone can recover the performance and nearly identical parameters of the fully fine-tuned model.
papers.conclusion: RL fine-tuning in LLMs naturally updates only a sparse subnetwork, driven by in-distribution training, enabling efficient recovery of full model performance via subnetwork-only fine-tuning and suggesting more efficient training strategies.
papers.key_findings:
RL induces sparse parameter updates (68.5% to 96% sparsity) across diverse algorithms and models without explicit regularization, while SFT induces dense updates.
Updates are distributed across all transformer layers and parameter matrices (Q, K, V, FFN) except layer normalization, which is rarely updated, and are sparse but full-rank.
Fine-tuning only the identified sparse subnetwork recovers the test accuracy and converges to nearly identical parameter values as the fully fine-tuned model.
Subnetworks show substantially higher overlap than random chance across different random seeds, training data, and RL algorithms, indicating a partially transferable structure.
The primary driver of update sparsity is training on in-distribution data (close to the policy distribution), while KL regularization and gradient clipping have limited impact.
papers.limitation:
The study varies one factor at a time, but the observed sparsity may result from complex interactions among many factors.
Fully controlled experiments are computationally prohibitive, leading to reliance on public checkpoints in some cases.
Experiments focus on language models; extending the analysis to multimodal and diffusion models is left for future work.
The empirical findings invite deeper theoretical analysis to explain the update sparsity phenomenon.
There are confounders (e.g., Liu et al. 2025a) that are not trivial and worth exploring in future work.
future_direction: Examine complex interactions among multiple factors contributing to update sparsity.
Explore the same sparsity phenomena in multimodal and diffusion models.
Investigate methods for early identification of the sparse subnetwork and leverage its structure for more efficient learning.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) yields substantial improvements in large language models (LLMs) downstream task performance and alignment with human values. Surprisingly, such large gains result from updating only a small subnetwork comprising just 5 percent to 30 percent of the parameters, with the rest effectively unchanged. We refer to this phenomenon as parameter update sparsity induced by RL. It is observed across all 7 widely used RL algorithms (e.g., PPO, GRPO, DPO) and all 10 LLMs from different families in our experiments. This sparsity is intrinsic and occurs without any explicit sparsity promoting regularizations or architectural constraints. Finetuning the subnetwork alone recovers the test accuracy, and, remarkably, produces a model nearly identical to the one obtained via full finetuning. The subnetworks from different random seeds, training data, and even RL algorithms show substantially greater overlap than expected by chance. Our analysis suggests that this sparsity is not due to updating only a subset of layers, instead, nearly all parameter matrices receive similarly sparse updates. Moreover, the updates to almost all parameter matrices are nearly full-rank, suggesting RL updates a small subset of parameters that nevertheless span almost the full subspaces that the parameter matrices can represent. We conjecture that the this update sparsity can be primarily attributed to training on data that is near the policy distribution, techniques that encourage the policy to remain close to the pretrained model, such as the KL regularization and gradient clipping, have limited impact.

papers.title: Efficiently Democratizing Medical LLMs for 50 Languages via a Mixture of Language Family Experts
papers.research_question: How to efficiently adapt medical Large Language Models to many languages, especially low-resource ones, by analyzing internal information flow and using language family experts?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an efficient method to scale medical LLMs to 50 languages via language family experts and a Post-MoE architecture, based on the discovery of the 'Spread Out in the End' information flow mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Apollo-MoE method efficiently democratizes medical LLMs to 50 languages, demonstrating strong generalization and scalability.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered the 'Spread Out in the End' mechanism in multilingual MoE models: early layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, later layers exhibit language-specific divergence.
Proposed Post-MoE architecture (MoE only in later layers) improves generalization to low-resource languages.
Introduced language family experts, enabling scaling to many languages without adding parameters.
Hybrid-k routing (language-specific experts with cross-lingual routing) outperforms Top-k and Language-Specific routing.
papers.abstract: Adapting medical Large Language Models to local languages can reduce barriers to accessing healthcare services, but data scarcity remains a significant challenge, particularly for low-resource languages. To address this, we first construct a high-quality medical dataset and conduct analysis to ensure its quality. In order to leverage the generalization capability of multilingual LLMs to efficiently scale to more resource-constrained languages, we explore the internal information flow of LLMs from a multilingual perspective using Mixture of Experts (MoE) modularity. Technically, we propose a novel MoE routing method that employs language-specific experts and cross-lingual routing. Inspired by circuit theory, our routing analysis revealed a Spread Out in the End information flow mechanism: while earlier layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, the later layers exhibit language-specific divergence. This insight directly led to the development of the Post-MoE architecture, which applies sparse routing only in the later layers while maintaining dense others. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enhances the generalization of multilingual models to other languages while preserving interpretability. Finally, to efficiently scale the model to 50 languages, we introduce the concept of language family experts, drawing on linguistic priors, which enables scaling the number of languages without adding additional parameters.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: Representation Disentaglement via Regularization by Causal Identification
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations by using causal identification to control dependencies between generating factors, especially in the presence of collider bias?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ReI, a regularization method that aligns deep learning models with causal identification constraints from a collider-structured DAG to achieve disentangled representations robust to out-of-distribution shifts.
papers.conclusion: ReI effectively disentangles representations by leveraging causal identification to control collider bias, leading to interpretable representations and robustness to dataset shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ReI outperforms existing disentanglement methods on standard benchmarks (dSprites, Shapes3D, MPI3D) in DCI metrics, especially when generative factors are correlated.
ReI produces representations that align with domain knowledge (e.g., spectral peaks for chemical elements) and are interpretable.
ReI shows improved robustness to out-of-distribution examples compared to standard VAEs in a real-world transfer task (Earth to Mars).
The collider DAG model explains entanglement as conditional dependencies between generating factors, which ReI controls via causal identification.
papers.limitation:
ReI requires a DAG model of the data generation process, which can be time-consuming to build.
When there are unobserved variables, causal identification may be challenging and may require approximations, potentially leaving residual entanglements.
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose the use of a causal collider structured model to describe the underlying data generative process assumptions in disentangled representation learning. This extends the conventional i.i.d. factorization assumption model $p(\mathbf{y}) = \prod_{i} p(\mathbf{y}_i )$, inadequate to handle learning from biased datasets (e.g., with sampling selection bias). The collider structure, explains that conditional dependencies between the underlying generating variables may be exist, even when these are in reality unrelated, complicating disentanglement. Under the rubric of causal inference, we show this issue can be reconciled under the condition of causal identification; attainable from data and a combination of constraints, aimed at controlling the dependencies characteristic of the \textit{collider} model. For this, we propose regularization by identification (ReI), a modular regularization engine designed to align the behavior of large scale generative models with the disentanglement constraints imposed by causal identification. Empirical evidence on standard benchmarks demonstrates the superiority of ReI in learning disentangled representations in a variational framework. In a real-world dataset we additionally show that our framework, results in interpretable representations robust to out-of-distribution examples and that align with the true expected effect from domain knowledge.

papers.title: Compositional Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: What kinds of abstractions are learned by neurons in deep models? Do compositional explanations give insight into model performance? Can they be used to predictably manipulate model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a procedure for generating compositional logical explanations of individual neurons, which provides more precise and expressive characterizations of neuron behavior than atomic labels, and applies it to analyze vision and NLP models.
papers.conclusion: Compositional explanations offer a more precise and expressive way to characterize neuron behavior, providing insights into model performance and enabling targeted adversarial manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons learn compositional concepts: in image classification, some learn meaningful perceptual abstractions while others are polysemantic; in NLI, shallow heuristics (e.g., based on gender, lexical overlap) are reified in individual neurons.
The interpretability of neurons correlates differently with performance: in image classification, human-interpretable abstractions are positively correlated with accuracy, while in NLI, neurons explained by shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with accuracy.
Compositional explanations enable the creation of simple 'copy-paste' adversarial examples that predictably change model behavior by targeting specific neurons.
papers.limitation:
The method requires technical expertise to implement, limiting usability by non-experts.
It relies on annotated datasets which may be expensive to collect and may be biased in the features they contain or omit.
Neuron-level explanations cannot identify concepts distributed across multiple neurons or establish definitive causal chains between inputs and decisions.
future_direction: Building easier user interfaces for explainability.
Reducing data annotation requirements.
Extending composition operators (e.g., to relations like ABOVE and BELOW) and applying the method to other tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We describe a procedure for explaining neurons in deep representations by identifying compositional logical concepts that closely approximate neuron behavior. Compared to prior work that uses atomic labels as explanations, analyzing neurons compositionally allows us to more precisely and expressively characterize their behavior. We use this procedure to answer several questions on interpretability in models for vision and natural language processing. First, we examine the kinds of abstractions learned by neurons. In image classification, we find that many neurons learn highly abstract but semantically coherent visual concepts, while other polysemantic neurons detect multiple unrelated features; in natural language inference (NLI), neurons learn shallow lexical heuristics from dataset biases. Second, we see whether compositional explanations give us insight into model performance: vision neurons that detect human-interpretable concepts are positively correlated with task performance, while NLI neurons that fire for shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with task performance. Finally, we show how compositional explanations provide an accessible way for end users to produce simple "copy-paste" adversarial examples that change model behavior in predictable ways.

papers.title: Representation Learning: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How can causal inference concepts formalize non-spuriousness and disentanglement in representation learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a causal framework to formally define non-spuriousness and disentanglement in representation learning.
papers.conclusion: A causal perspective provides a formal framework to define and enforce non-spuriousness and disentanglement in representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Non-spurious representations capture sufficient causes of labels, formalized using probabilities of sufficiency and necessity.
Efficient representations avoid redundant features, ensuring minimal sufficient causes.
Disentanglement requires independent features without causal connections in unsupervised learning.
papers.limitation: Not all causal quantities are observable from the data, making implementation challenging.
papers.abstract: Representation learning constructs low-dimensional representations to summarize essential features of high-dimensional data. This learning problem is often approached by describing various desiderata associated with learned representations; e.g., that they be non-spurious, efficient, or disentangled. It can be challenging, however, to turn these intuitive desiderata into formal criteria that can be measured and enhanced based on observed data. In this paper, we take a causal perspective on representation learning, formalizing desiderata like non-spuriousness and demonstrating their practical utility.

papers.title: The Low-Dimensional Linear Geometry of Contextualized Word Representations
papers.research_question: How are linguistic features encoded in the linear geometry of contextualized word representations, and what are the geometric properties of these encodings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional linear subspaces of contextualized word representations, that these subspaces have hierarchical structure and are distributed across neurons, and that they are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a probing procedure that reveals low-dimensional linear subspaces encoding linguistic features in word representations, with hierarchical and distributed structure, and shows these subspaces are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces of contextualized word representations.
These subspaces exhibit hierarchical structure (e.g., noun and verb subspaces nested within part-of-speech subspaces).
The subspaces are distributed across neurons rather than aligned with individual axes.
Ablating specific subspaces (e.g., nounspace or verbspace) impairs BERT's performance on subject-verb agreement, indicating causal relevance.
Contextual representations encode linguistic variables better but not more compactly than non-contextual word embeddings.
future_direction: Explore richer geometric structure in word representations and its effect on model behavior.
papers.abstract: Black-box probing models can reliably extract linguistic features like tense, number, and syntactic role from pretrained word representations. However, the manner in which these features are encoded in representations remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of the linear geometry of contextualized word representations in ELMO and BERT. We show that a variety of linguistic features (including structured dependency relationships) are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces. We then refine this geometric picture, showing that there are hierarchical relations between the subspaces encoding general linguistic categories and more specific ones, and that lowdimensional feature encodings are distributed rather than aligned to individual neurons. Finally, we demonstrate that these linear subspaces are causally related to model behavior, and can be used to perform fine-grained manipulation of BERT's output distribution.

papers.title: Transformers are efficient hierarchical chemical graph learners
papers.research_question: How can we design an efficient graph transformer that reduces computational cost and captures long-range interactions in molecular graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SubFormer, a graph transformer that combines hierarchical clustering and message-passing to efficiently learn graph representations, reducing computational cost and capturing long-range interactions while being competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: SubFormer performed consistently well on standard benchmarks for predicting molecular properties from chemical structures. Visualization of the attention maps suggests the model learns chemically pertinent features. SubFormer does not suffer from over-squashing, but over-smoothing remains an issue requiring further study.
papers.key_findings:
SubFormer is competitive with state-of-the-art graph transformers on molecular property prediction benchmarks at a fraction of the computational cost.
SubFormer attention weights correspond to chemically meaningful fragments (e.g., aromatic rings, charge-transfer fragments).
SubFormer does not suffer from over-squashing because attention allows direct long-range interactions.
SubFormer exhibits limited over-smoothing compared to GAT, but still experiences over-smoothing with increasing layers.
SubFormer is more expressive than the 1-WL test for graph isomorphism.
papers.limitation: Over-smoothing remains an issue, demanding further study.
future_direction: Further study to address over-smoothing.
Refine the graph decomposition strategy to improve separation power.
papers.abstract: Transformers, adapted from natural language processing, are emerging as a leading approach for graph representation learning. Contemporary graph transformers often treat nodes or edges as separate tokens. This approach leads to computational challenges for even moderately-sized graphs due to the quadratic scaling of self-attention complexity with token count. In this paper, we introduce SubFormer, a graph transformer that operates on subgraphs that aggregate information by a message-passing mechanism. This approach reduces the number of tokens and enhances learning long-range interactions. We demonstrate SubFormer on benchmarks for predicting molecular properties from chemical structures and show that it is competitive with state-of-the-art graph transformers at a fraction of the computational cost, with training times on the order of minutes on a consumer-grade graphics card. We interpret the attention weights in terms of chemical structures. We show that SubFormer exhibits limited over-smoothing and avoids over-squashing, which is prevalent in traditional graph neural networks.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.

papers.title: The Molecular Structure of Thought: Mapping the Topology of Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models learn and represent effective Long Chain-of-Thought?
papers.core_contribution: The paper models Long Chain-of-Thought as a molecular structure with three bond types and introduces Mole-Syn, a method to synthesize effective Long CoT structures, improving performance and RL stability.
papers.conclusion: The molecular structure view explains how LLMs learn Long CoT, and Mole-Syn enables effective synthesis of these structures for improved reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Long CoT reasoning exhibits stable molecular-like structures formed by deep-reasoning, self-reflection, and self-exploration bonds.
Semantic isomers with compatible bond structures are crucial for effective Long CoT learning, while incompatible structures lead to instability.
Distillation from strong reasoning LLMs successfully imparts Long CoT structures, but distillation from weak instruction LLMs or human traces fails.
Mole-Syn can synthesize effective Long CoT structures by transferring behavior distributions, boosting performance across benchmarks.
Conflict between two stable molecular structures during training causes structural chaos and degrades performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to learn effective long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning from human or non-Long-CoT LLMs imitation. To understand this, we propose that effective and learnable Long CoT trajectories feature stable molecular-like structures in unified view, which are formed by three interaction types: Deep-Reasoning (covalent-like), Self-Reflection (hydrogen-bond-like), and Self-Exploration (van der Waals-like). Analysis of distilled trajectories reveals these structures emerge from Long CoT fine-tuning, not keyword imitation. We introduce Effective Semantic Isomers and show that only bonds promoting fast entropy convergence support stable Long CoT learning, while structural competition impairs training. Drawing on these findings, we present Mole-Syn, a distribution-transfer-graph method that guides synthesis of effective Long CoT structures, boosting performance and RL stability across benchmarks.

papers.title: A Tale of Two Circuits: Grokking as Competition of Sparse and Dense Subnetworks
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism behind the grokking phase transition in neural networks, specifically how does competition between subnetworks lead to generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The grokking phase transition arises from competition between a sparse subnetwork and a dense subnetwork, driven by selective norm growth of neurons in the sparse subnetwork.
papers.conclusion: Grokking in neural networks is driven by competition between sparse and dense subnetworks, with selective norm growth leading to the emergence of a generalizing sparse subnetwork.
papers.key_findings:
Grokking corresponds to network sparsification, with a sparse subnetwork emerging to dominate predictions.
Selective norm growth of specific neurons induces sparsity during the grokking transition.
The sparse subnetwork competes with and eventually surpasses the dense subnetwork in controlling model output.
The size of the sparse subnetwork matches disjunctive normal form circuit sizes for computing parity.
Before grokking, the network may generalize based on task properties like commutativity, not just memorization.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to the specific setting of the sparse parity task.
future_direction: Extend analysis of grokking to large language models.
papers.abstract: Grokking is a phenomenon where a model trained on an algorithmic task first overfits but, then, after a large amount of additional training, undergoes a phase transition to generalize perfectly. We empirically study the internal structure of networks undergoing grokking on the sparse parity task, and find that the grokking phase transition corresponds to the emergence of a sparse subnetwork that dominates model predictions. On an optimization level, we find that this subnetwork arises when a small subset of neurons undergoes rapid norm growth, whereas the other neurons in the network decay slowly in norm. Thus, we suggest that the grokking phase transition can be understood to emerge from competition of two largely distinct subnetworks: a dense one that dominates before the transition and generalizes poorly, and a sparse one that dominates afterwards.

papers.title: Interpreting and Improving Adversarial Robustness of Deep Neural Networks With Neuron Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How does neuron sensitivity relate to adversarial robustness, and can stabilizing sensitive neurons improve model robustness against adversarial examples?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces neuron sensitivity as a measure for adversarial robustness and proposes the Sensitive Neuron Stabilizing (SNS) method to improve robustness by stabilizing the behaviors of sensitive neurons.
papers.conclusion: Neuron sensitivity is closely related to adversarial robustness, and stabilizing sensitive neurons can effectively improve model robustness against adversarial examples.
papers.key_findings:
Sensitive neurons (those with high behavior variation between benign and adversarial examples) make the most non-trivial contributions to model misclassification in adversarial settings.
State-of-the-art adversarial training methods improve model robustness by reducing neuron sensitivities.
Stabilizing sensitive neurons via the proposed SNS method effectively improves adversarial robustness across various datasets and attack methods.
There exists a trade-off between robustness and accuracy, and sensitive neurons are responsible for both clean accuracy and robustness.
Adversarial attacks exploit sensitive neurons differently at different layers, with bottom layers focusing on common low-level features and top layers on class-specific features.
papers.limitation:
Uses the same coefficient λ to combine sensitivities in different layers, which might not be optimal due to heterogeneous behaviors of different layers.
The layer selection method is a naive top-k procedure, which may not adapt well to various model architectures.
future_direction: Use adaptive coefficients that consider heterogeneous behaviors of different layers to make full use of each intermediate layer.
Develop a better layer selection strategy that adapts to various model architectures.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial examples where inputs with imperceptible perturbations mislead DNNs to incorrect results. Despite the potential risk they bring, adversarial examples are also valuable for providing insights into the weakness and blind-spots of DNNs. Thus, the interpretability of a DNN in the adversarial setting aims to explain the rationale behind its decision-making process and makes deeper understanding which results in better practical applications. To address this issue, we try to explain adversarial robustness for deep models from a new perspective of neuron sensitivity which is measured by neuron behavior variation intensity against benign and adversarial examples. In this paper, we first draw the close connection between adversarial robustness and neuron sensitivities, as sensitive neurons make the most non-trivial contributions to model predictions in the adversarial setting. Based on that, we further propose to improve adversarial robustness by stabilizing the behaviors of sensitive neurons. Moreover, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art adversarial training methods improve model robustness by reducing neuron sensitivities, which in turn confirms the strong connections between adversarial robustness and neuron sensitivity. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate that our algorithm effectively achieves excellent results. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study adversarial robustness using neuron sensitivities.

papers.title: Explaining the Behavior of Black-Box Prediction Algorithms with Causal Learning
papers.research_question: How can we provide causal explanations for black-box prediction models in terms of interpretable macro-level features, especially in the presence of unmeasured confounding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal discovery-based approach (using algorithms like FCI) to explain black-box model predictions in terms of interpretable macro-level features, which can handle unmeasured confounding and distinguish causal features from spurious associations.
papers.conclusion: Causal discovery methods provide a promising approach for explaining black-box models by identifying causal determinants of predictions in terms of interpretable features, advancing towards more trustworthy AI.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies stable causal macro-features for bird classification (e.g., Wing Shape, Wing Pattern) and pneumonia detection (e.g., Atelectasis, Infiltration).
